2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Supervi.what_it_is: The three broad paradigms of machine learning, distinguished by what kind of feedback the learner gets: supervised learning maps inputs to known labels/targets, unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, and reinforcement learning learns a policy by trial-and-error from delayed reward signals.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Supervi.why_it_exists: Different problems supply fundamentally different kinds of information — sometimes you have ground-truth answers (spam/not-spam), sometimes you only have raw observations and want to discover structure (customer segments), and sometimes the only signal is a scalar reward that arrives after a sequence of decisions (game playing, robotics). The taxonomy exists so you pick an algorithm family whose assumptions match the information you actually have.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Supervi.how_it_works: Supervised: learn f(x) ≈ y by minimizing a loss against labeled (x, y) pairs — classification (discrete y) or regression (continuous y). Unsupervised: no y at all; the objective is intrinsic to the data — clustering minimizes within-cluster variance, dimensionality reduction maximizes retained variance/information, density estimation models p(x). Reinforcement learning: an agent takes actions in an environment, observes state transitions and rewards, and learns a policy π(a|s) that maximizes expected cumulative (often discounted) reward — credit assignment over time is the central difficulty. Semi-supervised and self-supervised learning sit between these, using small labeled sets plus large unlabeled sets or auto-generated pretext tasks.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Supervi.use_when: Use supervised learning whenever you have reliable labels and the deployment task matches the labeled distribution (most business prediction problems). Use unsupervised learning for exploration, segmentation, anomaly detection, or as a pretraining/representation-learning step. Use RL when the problem is inherently sequential-decision-making with a reward signal and no fixed 'correct answer' dataset (control, recommendation as a sequential problem, game-playing).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Supervi.avoid_when: Don't force a supervised framing onto a problem where labels are expensive, noisy, or don't exist — you'll spend more effort on labeling than modeling. Don't reach for RL for problems that are really one-shot prediction tasks; RL is sample-inefficient and hard to debug, and a supervised or bandit formulation is usually simpler and more stable.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Supervi.what_goes_wrong: Mislabeling a problem: treating a ranking/sequential-decision problem as plain classification loses the temporal structure; treating clustering output as if it were ground truth (it isn't — cluster IDs are arbitrary and unstable across runs). In RL, reward shaping mistakes lead to agents that 'game' the reward instead of solving the intended task (reward hacking). In supervised learning, label leakage from the future or from the target itself silently inflates offline metrics.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Supervi.real_example: A churn-prediction project initially framed as supervised classification (label = churned within 30 days) discovered that 'next contact date' was populated only for churned customers — a leakage feature that gave 99% AUC offline and ~55% in production. Reframing with strict time-based splits and removing post-outcome features brought offline metrics in line with reality; a separate unsupervised RFM-segmentation model was kept as an exploratory tool for the marketing team, explicitly not used as a prediction signal.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Bias-va.what_it_is: A decomposition of a model's expected prediction error into three additive parts — bias² (error from overly simplistic assumptions), variance (error from sensitivity to the particular training sample), and irreducible noise — showing that reducing one of the first two often increases the other.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Bias-va.why_it_exists: It formalizes *why* both 'too simple' and 'too complex' models generalize poorly, giving a vocabulary for diagnosing and fixing generalization problems instead of randomly tweaking hyperparameters. It is the theoretical backbone behind regularization, ensembling, cross-validation, and the entire concept of model capacity.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Bias-va.how_it_works: For squared-error loss, E[(y − f̂(x))²] = Bias[f̂(x)]² + Var[f̂(x)] + σ². High-bias models (linear regression on nonlinear data, shallow trees) underfit — they make strong simplifying assumptions and the error is consistent across resamples. High-variance models (deep trees, k-NN with small k, high-degree polynomials) overfit — they chase noise in the training sample, so predictions swing wildly across resamples of the same population. Increasing model capacity typically lowers bias but raises variance; regularization, more data, and ensembling (bagging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias) shift the balance.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Bias-va.use_when: Use this lens whenever you're deciding how to respond to a gap between training and validation performance: high train error and high val error → high bias, simplify less / add capacity / add features; low train error and high val error → high variance, regularize, get more data, or ensemble (bagging).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Bias-va.avoid_when: Don't apply the classical decomposition literally to deep, overparameterized neural networks — empirically they can sit in a 'double descent' regime where increasing capacity past the interpolation threshold *reduces* test error, which the simple textbook curve doesn't predict. Use it as an intuition pump there, not a precise law.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Bias-va.what_goes_wrong: Teams chase 'more accuracy' by adding model complexity (more trees, deeper nets, more features) without checking whether the gap is a bias problem or a variance problem — making variance-dominated problems worse. Conversely, adding heavy regularization to an already high-bias model (e.g., strong L2 on an underfit linear model) further degrades performance. Misreading learning curves — e.g., calling a model 'high variance' when train and val curves have already converged but both plateau at a mediocre score (that's high bias / insufficient capacity or features).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Bias-va.real_example: A team saw their gradient-boosted model scoring 0.95 train AUC / 0.78 val AUC and concluded 'we need more data.' Plotting a learning curve showed val AUC was already flat with more data — the gap was variance from too many trees/too much depth, not data scarcity. Reducing max_depth and adding L2 regularization (reg_lambda) closed the gap to 0.85/0.83 and improved the val score, at a fraction of the cost of acquiring more labeled data.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Train /.what_it_is: The practice of partitioning labeled data into three disjoint sets — training (fit model parameters), validation (tune hyperparameters and make modeling decisions), and test (a final, untouched estimate of generalization performance) — with the test set used exactly once, at the very end.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Train /.why_it_exists: A model's performance on the data it was fit to is an optimistic, biased estimate of how it will do on new data. A single held-out set lets you estimate generalization, but if you also use that same set to make decisions (which model, which hyperparameters, which features), you implicitly fit to it — its performance estimate becomes biased too. The three-way split exists precisely to keep one slice 'clean' for an honest final readout.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Train /.how_it_works: Typical splits: 60/20/20 or 70/15/15 for small data; for large data, fixed-size val/test (e.g., 10K/10K rows) and the rest for training is common. Random splits assume i.i.d. data; for grouped data (multiple rows per user) use group-aware splitting so the same entity doesn't appear in both train and val/test; for temporal data use chronological splits so the model is never trained on the future. The validation set (or cross-validation folds) is used repeatedly during model/feature/hyperparameter search; the test set is touched only once, after all decisions are frozen, to report the number that will be trusted going forward.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Train /.use_when: Always, for any supervised model whose performance estimate matters for a go/no-go decision — which is essentially always in production ML. Use group-aware or time-aware splitting whenever rows are not independent (repeated measurements, panels, time series).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Train /.avoid_when: Skipping the held-out test set is acceptable only for quick exploratory prototyping that will be redone properly before any decision is made on it — never for a number that will be reported to stakeholders or used to choose between models.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Train /.what_goes_wrong: The most common violation: using the test set for early stopping, hyperparameter selection, or 'just checking' performance multiple times during development — each peek leaks information and inflates the reported score (this is sometimes called 'test set adaptive overfitting'). Other failures: random-splitting time series (training on the future, testing on the past — silent leakage); random-splitting grouped data (the same customer's rows end up in both train and test, so the model 'memorizes' the customer rather than generalizing); reporting validation-set performance as if it were test-set performance after having tuned extensively against it.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Train /.real_example: A Kaggle-style internal competition had teams iterating against a public leaderboard (effectively a validation set) hundreds of times; the team that 'won' on the public board dropped from rank 1 to rank 47 on the truly held-out private leaderboard — a textbook demonstration of adaptive overfitting to a repeatedly-queried set, which is exactly why production teams must keep a true, single-use test set.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|K-Fold,.what_it_is: A family of cross-validation splitting strategies in scikit-learn (`sklearn.model_selection`) that partition data into train/validation folds under different structural assumptions: plain K-Fold (random contiguous chunks), Stratified K-Fold (preserves class proportions), Group K-Fold (keeps groups intact across folds), and TimeSeriesSplit (expanding-window, chronological).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|K-Fold,.why_it_exists: A single train/val split gives one noisy estimate of generalization; cross-validation averages over multiple splits for a more stable estimate and uses the data more efficiently. But naive K-Fold assumes i.i.d. rows — which is violated by class imbalance, grouped/repeated-measure data, and temporal data — so specialized splitters exist to respect each structure and avoid leakage.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|K-Fold,.how_it_works: K-Fold: shuffles (optionally) and divides into k contiguous folds, training on k−1 and validating on the held-out fold, rotating. StratifiedKFold: same, but ensures each fold has approximately the same class distribution as the whole dataset — critical for imbalanced classification. GroupKFold: takes a `groups` array (e.g., user_id) and guarantees no group appears in both train and validation folds, preventing identity leakage. TimeSeriesSplit: produces folds where validation always comes chronologically after training (expanding window), mimicking real deployment where you predict the future from the past — never shuffles.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|K-Fold,.use_when: Use StratifiedKFold by default for classification (especially with any class imbalance); GroupKFold whenever multiple rows share an entity that could leak identity (patients, users, sessions); TimeSeriesSplit for any temporally ordered data; plain KFold only for i.i.d. regression data with no grouping structure.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|K-Fold,.avoid_when: Don't use plain shuffled KFold on time series (you'd train on the future and validate on the past) or on grouped data (identity leakage). Don't use StratifiedKFold for regression targets (no classes to stratify on — though `KBinsDiscretizer`-based stratification on binned targets is a common workaround for skewed regression targets).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|K-Fold,.what_goes_wrong: Using default KFold on grouped medical data lets the same patient's records land in both train and validation, producing inflated validation scores that collapse on truly new patients. Using shuffled KFold on time series causes 'lookahead bias' — the model implicitly learns from future data point statistics (e.g., scaling fit on the whole dataset before splitting), inflating validation metrics far above what chronological deployment will achieve. Forgetting to pass `groups=` to `GroupKFold.split()` silently falls back to ungrouped behavior in some pipelines.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|K-Fold,.real_example: A readmission-risk model cross-validated with plain KFold scored 0.91 AUC; switching to GroupKFold on patient_id dropped it to 0.79 — the 'true' number, because the original split had the same patients' historical and follow-up visits split across train and validation, letting the model partially memorize patient-specific patterns rather than learn generalizable risk factors.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Nested.what_it_is: A two-loop cross-validation procedure — an outer loop that estimates generalization performance and an inner loop (run independently within each outer training fold) that performs hyperparameter search — designed to produce an unbiased estimate of a *tuned* model's performance.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Nested.why_it_exists: If you tune hyperparameters using the same CV folds you then report performance on, the reported score is optimistic — you've effectively let the validation folds influence model selection, so they're no longer 'unseen.' Nested CV exists to give a statistically honest answer to 'how will my best, properly-tuned model perform on new data?' — separating the question of 'which hyperparameters are best' (inner loop) from 'how good is the tuning *process*' (outer loop).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Nested.how_it_works: Outer loop splits data into K folds; for each outer fold, the remaining K−1 folds go through an inner cross-validation (e.g., GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV) that selects the best hyperparameters using only that inner data; the resulting best model is then evaluated once on the outer held-out fold. Averaging the outer-fold scores gives an unbiased estimate of the *tuning pipeline's* expected performance — not of any single fixed hyperparameter set (those will likely differ slightly across outer folds, which is expected and fine).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Nested.use_when: Use nested CV when you need a defensible, publishable, or audit-grade estimate of how well your full model-selection-plus-tuning pipeline generalizes — e.g., comparing two algorithm families ('is XGBoost really better than logistic regression on this problem, after both are properly tuned?') or for small datasets where a single test set would be too noisy to trust.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Nested.avoid_when: Skip it for everyday iteration — it's K_outer × K_inner times more expensive than a single CV, which is often prohibitive for large datasets or expensive models (deep nets). For production purposes a simpler train/val/test split with a final held-out test set is usually sufficient once you've settled on an approach.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Nested.what_goes_wrong: Conflating nested CV's purpose: people sometimes try to extract 'the best hyperparameters' from the outer loop, but the outer loop's job is only to estimate performance — for a final deployable model, you re-run hyperparameter search on the *entire* dataset once nested CV has validated the approach. Computational blowup is the other common issue — naive nested CV with grid search can mean thousands of model fits, which is often infeasible without aggressive parallelism or a switch to randomized/Bayesian search in the inner loop.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Nested.real_example: A research team comparing random forests vs. gradient boosting for a clinical outcome used 5×3 nested CV (5 outer, 3 inner folds); the outer-loop estimates showed gradient boosting's apparent edge (reported via naive single-level CV) shrank to statistical insignificance once tuning bias was removed — saving the team from deploying a more complex, harder-to-maintain model for an illusory gain.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Overfit.what_it_is: Overfitting is when a model captures noise and idiosyncrasies of the training data rather than the underlying signal, performing well on training data but poorly on new data; underfitting is when a model is too simple to capture the underlying signal at all, performing poorly on both.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Overfit.why_it_exists: Every model has finite capacity relative to the complexity of the true data-generating process and the amount of training data; the gap between 'fits training data' and 'generalizes to new data' is the central practical problem of supervised learning, and the vocabulary of over/underfitting gives a shared diagnostic frame for addressing it.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Overfit.how_it_works: Diagnose via the gap between training and validation metrics, ideally visualized as learning curves (metric vs. training-set size) and validation curves (metric vs. a single hyperparameter like tree depth or regularization strength). Overfitting signature: low training error, much higher validation error, and the gap *persists or widens* as more data is added (though more data often helps). Underfitting signature: both training and validation error are high and close together — adding more data won't help; you need more capacity, better features, or less regularization. A 'good fit' shows both curves converging to a low, similar error as data grows.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Overfit.use_when: Run this diagnosis early and often — before reaching for more data, more compute, or a fancier algorithm, plot learning and validation curves to know *which* problem you actually have, since the fixes are often opposite (regularize vs. add capacity).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Overfit.avoid_when: Don't rely on a single train/test number without the curve — a single snapshot can't distinguish 'still improving with more data' from 'plateaued and overfitting.' Don't assume a small train-val gap always means a good model — both could simply be mediocre (underfitting).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Overfit.what_goes_wrong: Misreading a high-bias plateau as 'needs more data' wastes time and money collecting data that won't move the needle. Misreading high variance as 'needs a better algorithm' leads to swapping in ever more complex models that overfit even harder. A subtler failure: validation curves that look fine in aggregate can hide overfitting on specific subgroups (e.g., a minority class or rare segment) — slice-level diagnostics are needed to catch that.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Core Concepts|Overfit.real_example: A demand-forecasting model showed train MAPE 4% and validation MAPE 22% — classic overfitting. The team's first instinct was to collect more historical data (months of effort); plotting a learning curve first showed validation error was already flat past ~6 months of data — the real fix was reducing model complexity (fewer lag features, shallower trees) and adding L2 regularization, which closed the gap to 9%/11% in an afternoon.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|L.what_it_is: Engineered predictors that turn a time series' own history into tabular features for standard ML models — lag features (the value N steps ago) and rolling/window statistics (mean, std, min, max, etc., computed over a trailing window).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|L.why_it_exists: Most general-purpose ML algorithms (gradient boosting, random forests, linear models) have no innate notion of 'time' or sequence — they treat each row independently. To let them exploit temporal dependencies (autocorrelation, trend, seasonality, recent momentum), you must explicitly encode the relevant history as columns in the feature table.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|L.how_it_works: Lag features: `df['y_lag_1'] = df['y'].shift(1)`, `y_lag_7`, `y_lag_28`, etc., chosen to match known seasonal periods (daily, weekly). Rolling statistics: `df['y'].rolling(window=7).mean()`, `.std()`, `.min()/.max()`, optionally with `.shift(1)` first so the window doesn't include the current (unknown-at-prediction-time) value — this is the single most important detail to get right. Expanding windows (`.expanding()`) capture all-history statistics; exponentially weighted (`.ewm()`) give recency-weighted averages. These features are then fed into any tabular model (LightGBM, XGBoost, linear regression with regularization).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|L.use_when: Use this approach when you want to apply powerful general-purpose tabular models (which often outperform classical time-series models on problems with rich exogenous features) to forecasting or sequence-labeling problems, or when you need to combine temporal signal with non-temporal covariates (promotions, weather, prices).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|L.avoid_when: Avoid hand-crafted lags when the dependency structure is complex/long-range and a sequence model (LSTM, Temporal Fusion Transformer) or classical time-series model (ARIMA, ETS) that handles the recursion natively would be simpler and more accurate — and avoid them for very short series where lag features eat into the already-scarce usable rows (each lag of k removes k rows from the usable training set, or requires careful handling of the resulting NaNs).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|L.what_goes_wrong: The single most damaging bug: computing rolling statistics *without* shifting first, so the window includes the current row's target — this leaks the answer into the feature and produces beautiful offline metrics that evaporate in production ('rolling mean leakage'). Another: choosing lag/window lengths that don't match the data's actual seasonal structure (e.g., lag_7 on data with no weekly pattern) adds noise rather than signal. Forward-filling or otherwise imputing the NaNs created at the start of the series can also silently leak information if done across the train/validation boundary.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|L.real_example: A retail demand model used `df.groupby('store')['sales'].rolling(7).mean()` directly as a feature — which includes the current day's sales in its own 7-day average. Offline MAPE looked spectacular (3%); in production (where 'today's sales' obviously isn't known yet) it collapsed to 19%. Adding `.shift(1)` before `.rolling(7).mean()` fixed the leak and aligned offline and online metrics.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|T.what_it_is: A categorical-encoding technique that replaces each category with a statistic of the target variable for that category (typically the mean), computed in a cross-validated, out-of-fold manner specifically to avoid leaking each row's own target into its own encoded value.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|T.why_it_exists: High-cardinality categorical features (zip codes, product IDs, user IDs) blow up with one-hot encoding and aren't naturally ordered for ordinal encoding. Target encoding compresses each category into a single informative number tied directly to the prediction target — but doing it naively (using the *whole* dataset's mean per category, including the row being encoded) directly leaks the label into the feature, which is one of the most common sources of subtle overfitting in tabular ML.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|T.how_it_works: For each category c, the naive encoding is mean(y | category = c) computed over all rows — leaky. The CV-based fix: split the training data into K folds; for rows in fold k, compute the per-category target mean using only the *other* K−1 folds, then assign that out-of-fold mean to fold k's rows. Smoothing toward the global mean (`(n_c * cat_mean + m * global_mean) / (n_c + m)`) handles rare categories that would otherwise overfit to a handful of observations. At inference time, the encoding learned from the full training data (itself computed out-of-fold during fitting) is applied to new/unseen categories by falling back to the global mean. Libraries like `category_encoders.TargetEncoder` and `category_encoders.CatBoostEncoder` (which uses an ordered/online variant) implement this correctly.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|T.use_when: Use for high-cardinality categorical features in tree-based or linear models where one-hot encoding would be impractical, and where the category-target relationship carries real signal (e.g., merchant category codes for fraud, zip codes for housing price).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|T.avoid_when: Avoid when category cardinality is low (one-hot is simpler and leak-free) or when you have very little data per category (the encoding becomes noisy even with smoothing, and a simpler frequency or hashing encoding is safer).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|T.what_goes_wrong: The classic mistake: fitting the encoder on the full training set (including the row being transformed) before cross-validating the downstream model — this leaks target information through the encoding and inflates CV scores; the leak often only surfaces in production. Another failure: not handling unseen categories at inference (crashes or silently encodes as 0/NaN, degrading predictions for new products/users). Smoothing parameters chosen without validation can over- or under-shrink rare categories.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|T.real_example: A fraud model target-encoded `merchant_id` (50,000 distinct values) using the whole training set's fraud rate per merchant, then cross-validated — CV AUC was 0.97. Re-implementing with proper out-of-fold encoding (fit encoder only on the other folds for each fold's transform) dropped CV AUC to 0.89, which matched production performance much more closely — the 0.97 had been measuring how well the model memorized each merchant's historical fraud rate including the very transactions it was being scored on.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|P.what_it_is: Derived features formed by raising existing features to powers (x², x³) and/or multiplying pairs (or higher tuples) of features together (x₁·x₂), giving linear models access to nonlinear and combined effects without changing the underlying algorithm.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|P.why_it_exists: Linear models can only represent additive, linear relationships between each feature and the target in their raw form. Many real relationships are nonlinear (diminishing returns, thresholds) or involve *interactions* (the effect of feature A depends on the level of feature B — e.g., advertising spend matters more during holiday season). Polynomial/interaction features let you keep using simple, interpretable, fast linear models while still capturing such effects — at the cost of explicitly engineering them rather than letting the model discover them.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|P.how_it_works: `sklearn.preprocessing.PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, interaction_only=False)` generates all monomials up to the given degree (x₁, x₂, x₁², x₁x₂, x₂², …); `interaction_only=True` keeps only the cross terms (x₁x₂) and drops pure powers. The expanded feature set is then fed into a linear/logistic regression (often with regularization, since the feature count grows combinatorially — degree d over p features yields O(p^d) columns). Domain knowledge often beats brute-force expansion: hand-picking a few meaningful interactions (price × is_holiday) is usually more interpretable and less prone to overfitting than expanding everything.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|P.use_when: Use when you want to keep a linear/logistic-regression-style model (for speed, interpretability, or regulatory reasons) but suspect curvature or interaction effects in the data — common in pricing, risk scoring, and economics-style modeling where coefficients must be explainable.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|P.avoid_when: Avoid blind high-degree expansion on many features — the combinatorial explosion creates severe multicollinearity and overfitting risk, and tree-based models (which capture interactions and nonlinearity automatically via splits) are usually a better tool when interpretability constraints don't force a linear model.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|P.what_goes_wrong: Feature-count explosion: degree-3 expansion of 50 features produces tens of thousands of columns, causing memory blowup and severe overfitting unless paired with strong regularization (Lasso/Ridge) and dimensionality control. Multicollinearity between x, x², and interaction terms destabilizes coefficient estimates and their interpretation (this is why centering/scaling features before creating polynomial terms is standard practice). Forgetting to fit `PolynomialFeatures` only on training data (fitting on the full dataset before splitting) can leak distributional information about the validation/test set.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|P.real_example: A pricing-elasticity model needed to remain a linear model for regulatory explainability. Adding a single hand-chosen interaction term `price × is_competitor_promo` (rather than blanket degree-2 expansion of all 30 features) captured the key nonlinear effect — that price sensitivity roughly doubles during competitor promotions — improving R² from 0.61 to 0.74 while keeping the model to 31 interpretable coefficients instead of 496 from full polynomial expansion.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|F.what_it_is: Two lightweight techniques for converting categorical variables into numeric features without the dimensionality blowup of one-hot encoding: frequency encoding replaces each category with its occurrence count or proportion in the data, and the hashing trick maps categories to a fixed number of buckets via a hash function.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|F.why_it_exists: One-hot encoding a feature with thousands or millions of unique values (user IDs, URLs, product SKUs) is computationally infeasible and creates extremely sparse, high-dimensional inputs. Frequency encoding and hashing give compact, fixed-size numeric representations that scale to arbitrary cardinality — including categories never seen during training — at some cost in information fidelity.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|F.how_it_works: Frequency encoding: replace each category value with `count(category) / total_rows` (or raw count); this captures 'how common is this category' as a signal, which is often itself predictive (rare categories often correlate with anomalies or new entities). Hashing trick (`sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher`, or the hashing layers in TensorFlow/Keras): apply a hash function to each category string, take the result modulo a fixed bucket count B, and use the bucket index (optionally one-hot over B buckets) as the feature — collisions (different categories mapping to the same bucket) are accepted as a controlled trade-off for a fixed memory footprint that requires no fitted vocabulary and naturally handles unseen categories.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|F.use_when: Use frequency encoding as a cheap, leak-resistant baseline for medium-to-high cardinality categoricals (it requires no target information, so it's inherently leakage-free, unlike target encoding). Use the hashing trick for extremely high-cardinality or streaming/online settings where the category vocabulary is unknown in advance or too large to store (web-scale text features, online advertising).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|F.avoid_when: Avoid frequency encoding when category frequency itself isn't meaningfully related to the target (it can add noise rather than signal) and when two categories with similar frequency but very different target behavior get conflated. Avoid hashing when you need interpretability — hashed buckets are not traceable back to original categories, and collisions can silently merge semantically unrelated categories.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|F.what_goes_wrong: Frequency encoding computed on the full dataset (train+val+test combined) leaks distributional information about validation/test categories into training features — fit it on training data only, like any other transform. Hash collisions can disproportionately hurt rare-but-important categories (e.g., a rare fraud-associated merchant hashed into the same bucket as thousands of benign ones, diluting its signal) — bucket count must be chosen with collision rate in mind (`B` should be several times the expected number of unique categories).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|F.real_example: An ad-click model needed to encode `referrer_url`, with millions of distinct values and constant churn (new URLs appear hourly). One-hot encoding was infeasible; target encoding would require constant retraining of the encoder. Switching to `FeatureHasher` with 2^18 buckets gave a fixed-size, streaming-compatible feature with an acceptable ~0.4% collision-driven AUC cost (0.812 → 0.808) — a worthwhile trade for a pipeline that no longer needed daily vocabulary rebuilds.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.what_it_is: Derived features extracted from raw timestamp/date columns — day-of-week, month, quarter, hour-of-day, is_weekend, is_holiday, days-since-event, cyclical (sin/cos) encodings of periodic components — that expose calendar and seasonal structure to models that can't otherwise interpret a raw datetime.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.why_it_exists: Raw timestamps (e.g., Unix epoch integers or date strings) carry rich, human-meaningful periodic structure — weekly shopping patterns, monthly billing cycles, holiday spikes — that is invisible to a model unless decomposed into explicit components. Calendar effects are often among the most predictive features in retail, finance, operations, and web-traffic problems.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.how_it_works: Use `pandas` datetime accessors (`df['date'].dt.dayofweek`, `.dt.month`, `.dt.quarter`, `.dt.hour`, `.dt.is_month_end`) to extract integer/categorical components. Boolean flags like `is_weekend = dayofweek >= 5` and `is_holiday` (via a holiday calendar library, e.g. `holidays` or country-specific calendars, possibly with custom business-specific events) capture special days. Because raw integer encodings of cyclical features have a discontinuity (December=12, January=1 look 'far apart' to a linear model), cyclical encoding via `sin(2π·month/12)` and `cos(2π·month/12)` preserves the circular adjacency for models sensitive to numeric distance (linear models, neural nets); tree-based models handle raw integer encodings of cyclical features reasonably well via splits.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.use_when: Almost always for any time-stamped business data — sales, web traffic, transactions, sensor readings — where human/calendar rhythms plausibly drive the target. Use cyclical encodings specifically for linear/distance-based models; raw integer or one-hot encodings are usually fine for tree ensembles.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.avoid_when: Don't bother with elaborate calendar features for physical/sensor processes with no human-calendar dependency (e.g., raw equipment vibration at sub-second resolution) — the signal there comes from physics, not the Gregorian calendar. Avoid is_holiday flags built from a generic national calendar when the business's actual demand patterns follow different (e.g., regional, religious, or company-specific) calendars.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.what_goes_wrong: Treating month or day-of-week as a plain integer in a linear model introduces a spurious ordinal relationship (month 12 'far' from month 1) — use one-hot, cyclical encoding, or let a tree-based model handle it. Hard-coding a holiday list that goes stale (doesn't update for future years, or misses moving holidays like Easter/Lunar New Year) silently degrades forecasts on exactly the days that matter most. Time-zone bugs — extracting hour-of-day from UTC timestamps for a geographically distributed user base conflates very different local behaviors.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.real_example: A demand forecast for a US retailer used a generic `holidays.US()` calendar; it missed that the company's actual demand spikes followed a *promotional* calendar (Black Friday week, back-to-school) that didn't align with public holidays. Replacing the generic flag with custom `is_promo_week` / `days_to_next_promo` features — built from the marketing team's actual campaign calendar — improved forecast MAPE during peak weeks from 28% to 12%.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.what_it_is: Features hand-engineered from deep knowledge of a specific application domain — e.g., days-of-supply and stockout flags in inventory systems, price elasticity ratios in demand modeling, joint-torque and end-effector-pose derivatives in robotics — as opposed to generic statistical transforms applicable to any tabular dataset.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.why_it_exists: Generic features (lags, rolling stats, encodings) capture statistical regularities but not domain causality. A practitioner who understands *why* the target moves (a stockout suppresses observed demand; a robot's joint torque saturates near mechanical limits; price changes interact with promotional calendars) can encode that causal structure directly, often yielding far more predictive and robust features than anything an automated pipeline would discover from raw data alone — this is frequently what separates a mediocre model from a great one.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.how_it_works: There's no single recipe — it's the application of subject-matter expertise to feature construction. Examples: in demand forecasting, 'censored demand' correction (observed sales ≠ true demand when the product was out of stock, so raw sales must be adjusted using inventory/stockout records); in inventory, 'days of supply' = current_stock / average_daily_demand, and lead-time-adjusted reorder points; in robotics, derived kinematic/dynamic quantities (joint velocity and acceleration from position via finite differencing, contact-force estimates, manipulability indices) that encode physical constraints the raw sensor stream doesn't expose directly. The common thread: translating domain causal mechanisms into computable numeric features, often requiring collaboration with subject-matter experts (supply-chain planners, control engineers, clinicians).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.use_when: Whenever you have access to domain expertise (internal SMEs, established physical/economic models of the process) and the generic feature set has plateaued — domain features often provide the next big jump in performance after the 'easy' statistical features are exhausted.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.avoid_when: Don't over-invest in bespoke domain features early in a project, before establishing that a simpler generic-feature baseline is insufficient — they're expensive to build and maintain, and sometimes the generic approach is already good enough. Avoid encoding domain assumptions that may not hold across all segments/regions (a feature tuned to one warehouse's logistics may actively hurt predictions for another).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.what_goes_wrong: Using raw sales as a proxy for demand without correcting for stockouts systematically *underestimates* true demand for popular items (exactly the ones you most need accurate forecasts for) — a classic and costly inventory-forecasting mistake. In robotics, naively differentiating noisy position sensors to get velocity/acceleration amplifies noise catastrophically — proper filtering (Kalman filters, Savitzky-Golay) is required before the derived feature is usable. Domain features baked in by one expert can become silent technical debt — undocumented, fragile to upstream schema changes, and mysterious to whoever inherits the pipeline.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Engineering|D.real_example: A retailer's demand model trained directly on point-of-sale counts systematically under-forecast popular SKUs that frequently sold out — the model learned 'this SKU sells ~50/day' from days when it was actually capped by zero remaining stock, not true demand of ~80/day. Engineering a 'censored demand' feature (flagging stockout days and imputing corrected demand from comparable in-stock periods/stores) removed the downward bias and cut stockout-driven lost sales by an estimated 15% after the corrected forecasts drove larger reorder quantities.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Fil.what_it_is: A class of feature-selection techniques that score each feature's relationship to the target *independently of any model*, using statistical or information-theoretic measures — mutual information (general dependence, any data type), chi-square (association between categorical features and categorical targets), and ANOVA F-test (mean differences of a numeric feature across categorical target classes).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Fil.why_it_exists: Before training any model, you often want a fast, model-agnostic way to discard clearly irrelevant features — reducing dimensionality, training time, multicollinearity, and overfitting risk. Filter methods are the cheapest tier of feature selection: they require no model fitting, just a statistic per feature, computed in a single pass.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Fil.how_it_works: Mutual information (`sklearn.feature_selection.mutual_info_classif/regression`) estimates how much knowing the feature reduces uncertainty about the target — captures nonlinear dependencies, works for mixed types via k-NN-based estimators. Chi-square (`chi2`) tests independence between non-negative categorical/count features and a categorical target — requires non-negative inputs (so continuous features must be binned or scaled to [0, ∞)). ANOVA F-test (`f_classif` for classification, `f_regression` for regression) measures whether a numeric feature's means differ significantly across target classes (or correlates linearly with a numeric target) — assumes roughly normal, homoscedastic groups. All three produce a per-feature score/p-value that you rank and threshold, typically via `SelectKBest(score_func=..., k=...)` or `SelectPercentile`.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Fil.use_when: Use as a fast first-pass filter on high-dimensional data (text, genomics, wide tabular data) before more expensive wrapper/embedded methods, or whenever you need a quick sanity check on which raw features carry any signal at all.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Fil.avoid_when: Don't rely on filter methods alone for final feature selection — they evaluate each feature in isolation and miss interaction effects (two individually-useless features that are jointly predictive will both be discarded) and redundancy (ten correlated useful features all score highly and all get kept, when one would do).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Fil.what_goes_wrong: Choosing the wrong test for the data type — e.g., running chi-square on continuous, possibly-negative features without proper preprocessing throws errors or produces meaningless scores; ANOVA F-test on heavily skewed or non-normal numeric features can mis-rank due to violated assumptions. Setting an arbitrary `k` or percentile threshold without validating downstream model performance can discard genuinely useful features. Filter scores computed on the full dataset (including validation/test) leak distributional information.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Fil.real_example: A genomics classification task with 20,000 gene-expression features and 200 samples used mutual information filtering to cut to the top 500 features before training — reducing training time from hours to minutes and *improving* cross-validated accuracy from 0.71 to 0.79 by removing noise features that a full-dimensional model was overfitting to.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Wra.what_it_is: A feature-selection strategy that wraps a chosen estimator in a search loop: repeatedly train the model, rank features by an importance criterion (coefficients or feature_importances_), discard the least important one(s), and retrain — until a target number of features remains.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Wra.why_it_exists: Filter methods evaluate features in isolation and miss how they interact with a specific model; wrapper methods directly optimize for 'what subset of features makes *this* model perform best,' accounting for redundancy and interaction at the cost of being far more computationally expensive (many model refits).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Wra.how_it_works: `sklearn.feature_selection.RFE(estimator, n_features_to_select=k, step=1)` fits the estimator, ranks features by `coef_` magnitude (linear models) or `feature_importances_` (trees), removes the weakest `step` features, and repeats until k remain. `RFECV` wraps this in cross-validation to automatically choose the optimal number of features by validation score rather than a fixed k. Because each iteration requires a full model refit, cost scales roughly as O(n_features / step) model trainings — `step` can be increased (remove multiple features per round) to trade precision for speed on high-dimensional data.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Wra.use_when: Use when you have a moderate number of candidate features (tens to low hundreds), a reasonably fast-to-train base estimator, and want a feature subset specifically optimized for that estimator's behavior — common in regulated domains where a small, validated feature list is required for documentation/compliance.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Wra.avoid_when: Avoid on very high-dimensional data (thousands+ features) or with slow estimators (deep trees, large ensembles, neural nets) — the repeated refitting becomes prohibitively expensive; use embedded methods (L1, tree importances with a single fit) or filters first to cut down the candidate pool.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Wra.what_goes_wrong: RFE results are estimator-specific — a feature subset selected via RFE with a linear model may be suboptimal (or actively harmful) for a tree-based model, and vice versa; people sometimes select features with one model and deploy a different one. Feature importance instability (especially for correlated features in tree models, where importance gets split across correlated siblings) can make RFE's elimination order somewhat arbitrary run-to-run. Running RFE on the full dataset before cross-validating the final model leaks information about which features 'work' on the validation/test folds.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Wra.real_example: A credit-scoring team used `RFECV` with a logistic regression base estimator over 80 candidate features and 5-fold CV; it converged on 23 features with no loss in validation AUC (0.812 → 0.811) — a feature list small enough to satisfy the compliance team's requirement for a fully documented, auditable scorecard, which the original 80-feature model could not meet in a reasonable review timeframe.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Emb.what_it_is: Feature-selection mechanisms built directly into the model-fitting process itself — L1 (Lasso) regularization drives some linear-model coefficients exactly to zero during training, and tree-based ensembles produce a `feature_importances_` array as a natural byproduct of how often/how usefully each feature is used in splits.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Emb.why_it_exists: Filter methods ignore the model; wrapper methods refit the model many times. Embedded methods get feature selection 'for free' as part of a single model fit — capturing model-specific interactions and redundancy (unlike filters) without the combinatorial expense of wrapper search.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Emb.how_it_works: Lasso (`Lasso`, `LogisticRegression(penalty='l1')`, or `SGDClassifier(penalty='l1')`) adds an L1 penalty λ·Σ|wᵢ| to the loss; because the L1 penalty has a non-differentiable 'corner' at zero, the optimizer drives many coefficients to *exactly* zero (unlike L2/Ridge, which shrinks but rarely zeroes), yielding a sparse model where nonzero coefficients indicate selected features — `λ` (or `C` in sklearn's inverse-regularization parameterization) controls sparsity and is tuned via cross-validation (`LassoCV`). Tree ensembles (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) compute `feature_importances_` from how much each feature reduces impurity (Gini/entropy/variance) across all splits where it's used, weighted by the number of samples each split affects — `SelectFromModel(estimator, threshold=...)` then keeps features above an importance threshold.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Emb.use_when: Use Lasso when you want both sparsity (automatic feature selection) and a simple, interpretable linear model — common in high-dimensional, sparse-signal settings (genomics, text). Use tree feature_importances_ as a fast, no-extra-cost way to rank features after fitting a tree ensemble you were going to train anyway, e.g., as a first-pass screen or for stakeholder communication.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Emb.avoid_when: Avoid Lasso when features are highly correlated — it tends to arbitrarily pick one from a correlated group and zero out the rest, which can be unstable across resamples (Elastic Net, blending L1 and L2, mitigates this). Avoid over-trusting raw `feature_importances_` from default Gini/impurity-based scores when features have very different cardinalities or scales — high-cardinality categorical features get inflated importance purely from having more potential split points (permutation importance is a more robust alternative).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Emb.what_goes_wrong: Impurity-based `feature_importances_` are biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features (they offer more candidate split points, so trees use them more — even if randomly generated noise columns with high cardinality can score deceptively high). Lasso's feature selection is sensitive to feature scaling — unscaled features get unfairly penalized/favored based on their numeric range, so standardization before fitting is mandatory. People sometimes treat 'selected by Lasso/important per the tree' as proof of causal relevance, when it only reflects *predictive* association within this particular dataset and model.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Emb.real_example: A team ranking 200 marketing-mix features by Random Forest `feature_importances_` found a high-cardinality `campaign_id` (2,000 distinct values) at the top — outranking known business drivers like spend and seasonality. Switching to permutation importance (which measures the actual drop in held-out performance when a feature is shuffled) revealed `campaign_id`'s 'importance' was an artifact of its cardinality — its permutation importance was near zero, while spend and seasonality rose to the top, matching domain expectations.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Sel.what_it_is: Two scikit-learn utility transformers that operationalize feature selection as a pipeline step — `SelectKBest` keeps the top-k features by a univariate scoring function (filter-style), and `SelectFromModel` keeps features whose importance/coefficient from a fitted estimator exceeds a threshold (embedded-style) — both implementing the standard `fit`/`transform` interface so they slot directly into `Pipeline`.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Sel.why_it_exists: Feature selection needs to be a *reproducible, leak-free pipeline step* — fit on training folds only, applied consistently to validation/test/production data — rather than an ad-hoc one-off script. These transformers exist to make selection composable with the rest of the modeling pipeline (scaling, encoding, the final estimator) under scikit-learn's fit/transform contract, so cross-validation and grid search handle them correctly without manual bookkeeping.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Sel.how_it_works: `SelectKBest(score_func=f_classif, k=10)` computes a univariate score per feature (mutual information, chi-square, F-test — see filter methods) and keeps the top `k`; `SelectPercentile` is the same idea with a percentage cutoff. `SelectFromModel(estimator, threshold='median')` fits (or accepts a pre-fitted) estimator, reads `coef_` or `feature_importances_`, and keeps features above the threshold (which can be a number, `'mean'`, `'median'`, or a scaled string like `'1.25*mean'`). Both expose `get_support()` to recover which original columns survived, and both are designed to live inside a `Pipeline([('select', SelectKBest(...)), ('clf', estimator)])` so that `cross_val_score`/`GridSearchCV` correctly refit the selector within each fold — preventing leakage.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Sel.use_when: Use these whenever you want feature selection to be part of a reproducible, cross-validation-safe pipeline — which should be essentially always, instead of selecting features once on the full dataset and then cross-validating only the downstream model.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Sel.avoid_when: Don't use `SelectKBest` with a fixed `k` chosen by eye — wrap it in a grid search over `k` (or use `SelectPercentile` with a tuned percentile) so the choice is validated rather than guessed. Don't use `SelectFromModel` with an estimator type mismatched to your final model (selecting via a linear model's coefficients, then deploying a tree ensemble) without checking that the selected subset still helps the deployed model.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Sel.what_goes_wrong: The most damaging and common mistake: calling `selector.fit(X, y)` on the *entire* dataset (including validation/test) before cross-validating the downstream model — this leaks target information from the held-out folds into the feature-selection decision, inflating CV scores. The fix is always to put the selector inside a `Pipeline` so it's refit within each CV fold. Another pitfall: `SelectFromModel`'s default `threshold='mean'` can be too aggressive or too lenient depending on the importance distribution's shape — it should be tuned, not assumed.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Sel.real_example: A team built `pipe = Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('select', SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=20)), ('clf', LogisticRegression())])` and ran `GridSearchCV` over both `select__k` and `clf__C` simultaneously — discovering that k=35 (not their initially-guessed k=20) gave the best cross-validated F1, and that doing the search jointly (rather than fixing k first via a separate, leaky pre-selection step) avoided a 4-point CV/test gap they'd seen in an earlier, non-pipelined version.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Var.what_it_is: A diagnostic statistic that quantifies how much a regression coefficient's variance is inflated due to linear correlation with the other predictors — VIF(xᵢ) = 1 / (1 − R²ᵢ), where R²ᵢ is the R² of regressing xᵢ on all other features.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Var.why_it_exists: Multicollinearity (predictors that are linear combinations or near-combinations of each other) doesn't necessarily hurt a linear model's *predictions*, but it makes individual coefficient estimates unstable, inflates their standard errors, and can flip their signs — destroying interpretability and making statistical inference (p-values, confidence intervals) unreliable. VIF gives a per-feature, interpretable number for *how bad* the collinearity is, so you know which features to merge, drop, or regularize away.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Var.how_it_works: For each feature xᵢ, fit a linear regression of xᵢ on all other features, take its R², and compute VIF = 1/(1−R²). VIF=1 means no correlation with other predictors; VIF=5 means the variance of that coefficient is 5× what it would be with no collinearity; common rule-of-thumb thresholds flag VIF > 5 or VIF > 10 as problematic (these are heuristics, not hard laws — context matters). `statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence.variance_inflation_factor` computes this directly; remediation options include dropping one of a highly-correlated pair, combining correlated features (PCA, sums/ratios that are domain-meaningful), or switching to regularized regression (Ridge handles correlated predictors gracefully without dropping any).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Var.use_when: Use when you need interpretable, stable coefficients from a linear/logistic regression — econometrics, causal inference, regulated scoring models, A/B-test covariate adjustment — and want to diagnose *why* coefficients look unstable or counter-intuitive (wrong sign, huge swings across resamples).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Var.avoid_when: Don't bother computing VIF if your goal is pure prediction with a model that handles correlated features natively (tree ensembles, regularized regression, neural nets) — multicollinearity barely affects their predictive accuracy, only (for linear models) the interpretability of coefficients.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Var.what_goes_wrong: Treating VIF thresholds as hard cutoffs rather than heuristics — blindly dropping every feature with VIF > 10 can remove genuinely useful predictors (especially in models with many naturally-correlated domain features, like macroeconomic indicators). Computing VIF on data that includes the target or on a non-regression context (it's specifically a linear-regression-on-predictors diagnostic) produces meaningless numbers. Ignoring *why* features are correlated — sometimes the fix is to engineer a single combined feature (e.g., 'BMI' from height and weight) rather than mechanically dropping one.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Feature Selection|Var.real_example: A housing-price regression had wildly unstable coefficients for `total_sqft` and `num_rooms` (sign flipping between resamples) — VIF for both exceeded 18. Rather than dropping either (both carry real, distinct information), the team engineered `sqft_per_room = total_sqft / num_rooms` and `total_sqft` alone, which cut both VIFs below 4, stabilized the coefficients across bootstrap resamples, and made the model's pricing logic explainable to the business stakeholders who needed to sign off on it.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Missing.what_it_is: Techniques for filling in missing values in a dataset before model training — ranging from simple constant/statistic-based imputation (mean, median, mode) to similarity-based (`KNNImputer`, filling using the values of the k nearest complete rows) to model-based iterative imputation (`IterativeImputer`, which models each feature with missing values as a function of the other features in a round-robin fashion, à la MICE).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Missing.why_it_exists: Most ML algorithms cannot handle NaNs natively (some tree libraries like LightGBM/XGBoost/CatBoost are exceptions with built-in missing-value handling), and simply dropping incomplete rows/columns can throw away large fractions of usable data or introduce bias if 'missingness' itself correlates with the outcome. Imputation exists to retain that data while providing the model with *some* reasonable value — the right choice depends on how much structure there is in the missingness and how much accuracy improvement justifies the added complexity.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Missing.how_it_works: Mean/median imputation (`SimpleImputer(strategy='mean'/'median'/'most_frequent')`) replaces missing entries with that column's central tendency from the *training* data — fast, simple, but ignores relationships between features and shrinks variance. `KNNImputer(n_neighbors=k)` finds the k rows most similar (by the *non-missing* features, using a NaN-aware distance metric) and averages their values for the missing entries — captures local structure but is computationally expensive at scale and sensitive to feature scaling. `IterativeImputer` (scikit-learn's experimental MICE-style implementation) models each feature with missing values as a regression target on all other features, cycling through features multiple times until convergence — captures multivariate structure best but is the slowest and most complex to tune. All three must be `fit` on training data only and `transform`-applied to validation/test/production to avoid leakage, and ideally wrapped with a `MissingIndicator` column flagging *where* values were missing (since missingness can itself be predictive).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Missing.use_when: Use mean/median for quick baselines or when missingness is rare and presumed random (MCAR). Use KNNImputer or IterativeImputer when missingness is more substantial and you suspect the missing values are related to other observed features (MAR) — they recover more signal at higher computational cost. Always consider adding a missing-indicator feature alongside any imputation.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Missing.avoid_when: Avoid elaborate imputation when a simpler approach (native NaN-handling tree models, or simply dropping a column that's >70-80% missing) would do — added pipeline complexity has a maintenance cost. Avoid mean/median imputation for features with strong skew or multimodality — it can create an artificial spike at the imputed value that confuses some models (especially density-based or distance-based ones).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Missing.what_goes_wrong: Fitting an imputer on the full dataset (train+val+test) rather than training data only leaks distributional information. Imputation that ignores *why* data is missing can introduce systematic bias — e.g., income is often missing precisely for the unemployed or very wealthy (informative missingness, MNAR), and mean-imputing it erases exactly the signal that mattered. Heavy reliance on KNN/Iterative imputers on large datasets can make pipelines prohibitively slow, especially when nested inside cross-validation/hyperparameter search loops (each fold refits the imputer).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Missing.real_example: A loan-default model had 18% missing values in `annual_income`. Mean imputation gave AUC 0.71. Investigating *why* it was missing revealed two distinct populations — self-employed applicants (who often don't report a fixed salary) and a data-entry glitch affecting one branch's submissions. Adding a `MissingIndicator` for `annual_income` plus `IterativeImputer` conditioned on employment type and branch raised AUC to 0.77 — the missingness pattern itself, once made explicit, was informative.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|One-hot.what_it_is: A spectrum of techniques for converting categorical (non-numeric) variables into numeric form for ML models — one-hot encoding (a binary indicator column per category), ordinal encoding (integer codes reflecting a meaningful order), target encoding (replace category with a target-derived statistic), and frequency encoding (replace category with its occurrence rate) — each making different trade-offs between dimensionality, leakage risk, and how much ordering/structure they impose.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|One-hot.why_it_exists: Virtually all ML algorithms operate on numbers, but a huge fraction of real-world data is categorical (country, product type, browser, diagnosis code). The choice of encoding is not cosmetic — it materially shapes what relationships a model *can* represent (one-hot imposes no order; ordinal imposes a possibly-false order; target/frequency compress cardinality into informative scalars at different leakage/interpretability costs), so picking the right one for the cardinality, the model family, and the data's actual structure is a core modeling decision.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|One-hot.how_it_works: One-hot (`OneHotEncoder`, `pd.get_dummies`): creates a binary column per category — no false ordinal assumption, but blows up dimensionality for high-cardinality features and creates sparse, collinear columns (drop one category to avoid the 'dummy variable trap' for linear models). Ordinal (`OrdinalEncoder`): maps categories to integers — appropriate *only* when categories have a true inherent order (low/medium/high; education level), since linear/distance-based models will otherwise interpret the integers as having false magnitude relationships. Target encoding: replaces each category with a (cross-validated, smoothed) statistic of the target — see [[Target encoding (CV-based to prevent leakage)]] for the leakage-prevention details. Frequency encoding: replaces each category with its occurrence count/rate — leak-free (uses no target information) and naturally compact for high cardinality.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|One-hot.use_when: Use one-hot for low-to-medium cardinality nominal (unordered) categories, especially with linear models or neural nets. Use ordinal only for genuinely ordered categories, or as a cheap default for tree-based models (which can recover arbitrary groupings via splits regardless of the imposed order, making the 'false order' concern much less severe than for linear models). Use target/frequency encoding for high-cardinality nominal features where one-hot would be impractical.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|One-hot.avoid_when: Avoid ordinal encoding of unordered categories feeding into linear or distance-based models (introduces a fictitious metric structure). Avoid one-hot encoding very high-cardinality features (memory blowup, sparse curse-of-dimensionality). Avoid target encoding without cross-validated, leak-resistant implementation (see the dedicated note on that risk).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|One-hot.what_goes_wrong: Ordinal-encoding a nominal feature like `color` as {red:0, green:1, blue:2} silently tells a linear model that 'blue is twice green,' a meaningless and harmful relationship. One-hot encoding a 50,000-category `user_id` produces a 50,000-column sparse matrix that blows memory and trains glacially while adding little generalizable signal (each category has too few examples). Inconsistent encoding between training and serving (e.g., the one-hot encoder fit on training data doesn't know about a brand-new category seen in production) crashes or silently zeros out the feature — `handle_unknown='ignore'` in `OneHotEncoder` is essential for production robustness.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|One-hot.real_example: An early version of a customer-segmentation model ordinal-encoded `subscription_plan` as {Free:0, Basic:1, Pro:2, Enterprise:3} fed into a k-means clustering — distance-based, so it implicitly assumed Enterprise customers are '3x' Free customers along that dimension, distorting cluster shapes. Switching to one-hot encoding (since the four plans aren't on a single linear scale of 'customer value' from the clustering algorithm's perspective) produced visibly more coherent, business-interpretable segments that matched the sales team's intuitive groupings.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Standar.what_it_is: A family of scikit-learn transformers (`sklearn.preprocessing`) that rescale numeric features to comparable ranges — `StandardScaler` (zero mean, unit variance via z-score), `MinMaxScaler` (rescale to a fixed range, typically [0,1]), `RobustScaler` (centers/scales using median and interquartile range, resistant to outliers), and `QuantileTransformer` (maps feature distributions to a uniform or normal target distribution via rank-based transformation).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Standar.why_it_exists: Many algorithms — gradient descent-based models (linear/logistic regression, neural nets), distance-based models (k-NN, k-means, SVMs), and PCA — are sensitive to the *scale* of input features: a feature measured in thousands will dominate a loss function or distance calculation over one measured in single digits, regardless of its actual predictive importance, and gradient descent converges far more slowly/unstably on poorly-scaled inputs. Scalers exist to put features on comparable footing so the algorithm — and the practitioner reading its outputs (coefficients, distances) — isn't misled by arbitrary measurement units.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Standar.how_it_works: `StandardScaler`: (x − mean) / std, computed from training data; assumes roughly symmetric distributions and is sensitive to outliers (which inflate the std and compress the rest of the data toward zero). `MinMaxScaler`: (x − min) / (max − min), bounded output range; very sensitive to outliers (a single extreme value compresses everything else). `RobustScaler`: (x − median) / IQR; ignores outliers by construction, making it the safer default for messy real-world data with heavy tails. `QuantileTransformer`: ranks values and maps them to quantiles of a target distribution (uniform or normal), which is a nonlinear, monotonic transform that handles skew and outliers aggressively but distorts linear relationships and correlations between features (use cautiously for models that rely on linear structure). All scalers must be `fit` on training data only and `transform`-applied elsewhere — `Pipeline` integration prevents leakage automatically.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Standar.use_when: Use `StandardScaler` as the default for roughly-Gaussian features feeding gradient-descent or distance-based models. Use `RobustScaler` when data has significant outliers (financial, sensor, or web-traffic data often does). Use `MinMaxScaler` when you need bounded outputs (e.g., for neural net activation ranges, or image pixel data). Use `QuantileTransformer` for heavily skewed features where you need to break the influence of extreme tails and don't depend on preserving linear relationships.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Standar.avoid_when: Skip scaling entirely for tree-based models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) — they split on raw thresholds and are invariant to monotonic feature transforms, so scaling adds pipeline complexity with zero benefit. Avoid `MinMaxScaler`/`StandardScaler` on heavy-tailed data without first checking for outliers — a single data-entry error (e.g., age = 999) can silently compress the entire rest of the feature's useful range.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Standar.what_goes_wrong: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset (train+test) before splitting leaks distributional statistics (mean, std, min, max, quantiles) of the test set into the training pipeline — always fit on training folds only, ideally inside a `Pipeline`. Forgetting to scale before distance-based or gradient-based algorithms causes features with large numeric ranges to dominate, masking the signal in smaller-scale (but possibly more predictive) features. Mixing scaler choice with model assumptions — e.g., using `QuantileTransformer(output_distribution='normal')` and then interpreting linear-regression coefficients as if they reflected the original units — produces results that are difficult to explain to stakeholders.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Standar.real_example: A k-means customer-segmentation pipeline fed raw features including `annual_income` (range: $20K–$500K) and `num_logins_per_week` (range: 0–30). Distance calculations were completely dominated by income — clusters essentially just bucketed customers by income decile, ignoring engagement entirely. Applying `RobustScaler` (chosen over `StandardScaler` because income was heavily right-skewed with a few high-net-worth outliers) put both features on comparable footing, producing clusters that visibly separated by *both* income and engagement — which is what the marketing team actually needed for targeting.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Power t.what_it_is: Parametric, monotonic transformations — Box-Cox and Yeo-Johnson (`sklearn.preprocessing.PowerTransformer`) — that reshape a skewed numeric distribution toward a more Gaussian (symmetric, homoscedastic) one by raising values to a data-driven power λ, chosen via maximum likelihood.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Power t.why_it_exists: Many statistical and ML methods (linear regression, LDA, some distance-based methods) assume or perform best with roughly normal, homoscedastic (constant-variance) features/residuals — assumptions frequently violated by real-world data (incomes, durations, counts, prices are often right-skewed). Power transforms provide a principled, automatic way to find the 'best' reshaping power rather than guessing between ad-hoc options like log, square-root, or reciprocal transforms.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Power t.how_it_works: Box-Cox: y(λ) = (yᵏ − 1)/λ for λ≠0, log(y) for λ=0 — but requires strictly positive input values, which limits its applicability. Yeo-Johnson: a generalization that handles zero and negative values by using a piecewise definition split on the sign of y, making it usable on arbitrary real-valued features. Both methods estimate the optimal λ via maximum likelihood on the training data (`PowerTransformer(method='box-cox'/'yeo-johnson', standardize=True)`), and by default also standardize the output to zero mean/unit variance. The chosen λ is a property of the *training* fit and must be reused (not re-estimated) on validation/test/production data.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Power t.use_when: Use when a feature (or target, in regression) is heavily skewed and you're using a model or method that benefits from near-Gaussian inputs — linear/logistic regression, LDA/QDA, Gaussian-process kernels, or any pipeline step (PCA) sensitive to variance structure. Prefer Yeo-Johnson by default since it handles zero/negative values; use Box-Cox only when you know all values are strictly positive and want its specific (slightly more interpretable, single-parameter) form.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Power t.avoid_when: Skip power transforms for tree-based models — they're invariant to monotonic transforms of individual features, so the extra step adds complexity without benefit. Avoid applying them blindly to features that are already roughly symmetric (can introduce *new* skew or distort meaningful structure) or to categorical/count data better handled by other encodings (Poisson/negative-binomial structure, log1p for sparse non-negative counts).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Power t.what_goes_wrong: Estimating λ on the full dataset (or worse, separately on train and test) creates leakage or train/serve skew — fit once on training data, apply that same λ everywhere downstream. Over-applying transforms 'just in case' to every numeric feature can actually hurt tree-based or already-robust models, and makes coefficients/feature importances harder to interpret in their transformed units. Forgetting that the transform must be inverted (`inverse_transform`) when the *target* was transformed for regression — reporting predictions in transformed-space units to business stakeholders who expect original units is a common, confusing mistake.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Power t.real_example: A regression model predicting `claim_amount` (heavily right-skewed, with a long tail of large claims) had heteroscedastic residuals and poor calibration for large claims. Applying Yeo-Johnson to the target before fitting (and inverse-transforming predictions back to dollar amounts for reporting) stabilized residual variance across the prediction range and improved the model's calibration on the largest 5% of claims — the segment the business cared most about getting right — without changing the underlying linear model.

2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Scikit-.what_it_is: Two composability primitives in scikit-learn — `Pipeline` chains a sequence of transform/estimator steps into a single object with a unified `fit`/`predict` interface, and `ColumnTransformer` applies different preprocessing to different subsets of columns (numeric vs. categorical vs. text) and concatenates the results — together forming the standard way to assemble a leak-free, reproducible, deployable preprocessing-plus-model workflow.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Scikit-.why_it_exists: Real tabular datasets need different treatment for different column types (scaling for numerics, encoding for categoricals, vectorizing for text), and every one of those steps must be `fit` only on training folds and consistently `transform`-applied to validation/test/production to avoid leakage. Doing this by hand with separate fit/transform calls is tedious and a frequent source of leakage bugs (fitting a scaler on the full dataset, forgetting to apply the same encoder to test data, mismatched column ordering). `Pipeline`/`ColumnTransformer` encode this discipline structurally — the *correct* leak-free behavior becomes the path of least resistance, and the whole thing can be cross-validated, grid-searched, pickled, and deployed as one unit.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Scikit-.how_it_works: `ColumnTransformer([('num', StandardScaler(), numeric_cols), ('cat', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'), categorical_cols)])` routes each column subset to its own transformer and horizontally stacks the outputs. Wrapping that in `Pipeline([('preprocess', column_transformer), ('model', estimator)])` produces a single object: calling `.fit(X_train, y_train)` fits *every* step (including the preprocessing) using only training data, and `.predict(X_new)` runs the *exact same* fitted transformations before the final estimator — guaranteeing train/serve consistency. `cross_val_score`/`GridSearchCV` operate on the whole pipeline, so each CV fold independently refits the preprocessing — eliminating an entire class of leakage bugs by construction. Hyperparameters of nested steps are addressed with the `step_name__param` syntax (e.g., `model__C`, `preprocess__num__with_mean`).
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Scikit-.use_when: Use this as the default architecture for essentially any scikit-learn-based tabular ML project — it should be the *first* thing you reach for, not a refactor applied later, since retrofitting leak-free behavior onto ad-hoc preprocessing code is much harder than building it in from the start.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Scikit-.avoid_when: The pattern has essentially no downside for scikit-learn-compatible workflows; the only friction is when you need preprocessing logic that doesn't fit the `fit`/`transform` contract (highly stateful, cross-row dependent transforms) — at which point custom `FunctionTransformer`/`BaseEstimator`/`TransformerMixin` subclasses extend the same framework rather than abandoning it.
2|🔴 T1 ML Workflow|Preprocessing|Scikit-.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting `handle_unknown='ignore'` on `OneHotEncoder` inside a `ColumnTransformer` causes production crashes the moment a brand-new category appears. Mismatches between the column lists passed to `ColumnTransformer` and the actual columns present at inference time (schema drift) raise cryptic errors or silently misroute columns.
