2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_it_is: The component of a Generalized Linear Model that connects the linear predictor η = Xβ (an unrestricted real number) to the mean of the response distribution μ via an invertible function g, such that g(μ) = η — common choices include the identity link (g(μ)=μ, for Gaussian/linear regression), the logit link (g(μ)=log(μ/(1−μ)), for Bernoulli/logistic regression), the log link (g(μ)=log(μ), for Poisson/Gamma regression), and the inverse link (g(μ)=1/μ, for some Gamma/inverse-Gaussian formulations).
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.why_it_exists: A linear combination Xβ can produce any real number, including negative values — but many target distributions have constrained means (counts and positive quantities must have μ > 0; probabilities must have 0 < μ < 1). The link function exists to bridge this gap: it maps the constrained mean μ onto the unconstrained real line where linear modeling makes sense, ensuring that whatever Xβ predicts, the back-transformed μ = g⁻¹(Xβ) always respects the response distribution's natural constraints.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.how_it_works: Identity link (g(μ)=μ): used for Gaussian responses where μ can be any real number — this reduces the GLM exactly to ordinary linear regression. Logit link (g(μ)=log(μ/(1−μ))): used for Bernoulli/Binomial responses where μ ∈ (0,1) — maps probabilities to log-odds, which range over all reals; its inverse is the familiar sigmoid function, making this the link underlying logistic regression. Log link (g(μ)=log(μ)): used for Poisson/Gamma responses where μ > 0 — maps positive means to all reals; its inverse, the exponential function, guarantees predictions are always positive, and gives coefficients a natural multiplicative ('a one-unit increase in x multiplies the expected count by e^β') interpretation. Inverse link (g(μ)=1/μ): occasionally used with Gamma responses, mapping positive means to positive reals (less commonly chosen than the log link in practice, partly because its coefficient interpretation is less intuitive). Each distribution family has a 'canonical' link (the one matching its natural exponential-family parameter) that has favorable mathematical properties for estimation, but other valid links can be chosen when they better match domain interpretation needs.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.use_when: Choose the link function based on the natural range of your target's mean: identity for unconstrained continuous targets, logit for probabilities/binary outcomes, log for strictly-positive targets (counts, durations, monetary amounts) where you also want naturally multiplicative coefficient interpretations.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.avoid_when: Avoid the identity link for targets with a constrained range (counts, probabilities, positive amounts) — it permits the linear predictor to imply impossible values (negative counts, probabilities outside [0,1]), producing nonsensical predictions at the extremes of the input range, even if the fitted model 'looks fine' near the bulk of the data.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_goes_wrong: Using the identity link for a Poisson-style count model can produce negative predicted counts for some input combinations — a logically impossible result that surfaces (often embarrassingly) only when the model is queried on unusual or extreme inputs. Misinterpreting log-link coefficients as if they were additive (identity-link-style) effects — they're actually multiplicative on the original scale (a coefficient of 0.1 means 'multiply the expected value by e^0.1 ≈ 1.105,' i.e., roughly a 10.5% increase, not 'add 0.1') — is a frequent and substantively misleading communication error. Choosing a non-canonical link without understanding the resulting changes to estimation properties and interpretation can introduce subtle convergence or interpretability issues that canonical links avoid by construction.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.real_example: An early version of a hospital length-of-stay model used identity-link (ordinary linear regression) on a target that's strictly positive and right-skewed; for a subset of low-acuity patient profiles, it predicted *negative* expected lengths of stay — a result that immediately undermined clinical staff's trust in the entire system. Switching to a Gamma GLM with a log link guaranteed all predictions were positive by construction, and reframed coefficients in natural multiplicative terms ('this comorbidity multiplies expected stay by 1.3x') that clinicians found more intuitive than the original additive framing — fixing both the technical flaw and the communication problem in one change.

2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_it_is: A Generalized Linear Model specifically for modeling non-negative integer count data — number of customer arrivals, units sold, defects per batch, website hits per hour — using the Poisson distribution (which assumes variance equals the mean) combined with a log link function, fit via `statsmodels.GLM(family=sm.families.Poisson())` or `sklearn.linear_model.PoissonRegressor`.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.why_it_exists: Counts have structural properties that ordinary linear regression handles poorly: they're non-negative integers (a Gaussian model can predict negative or fractional counts), their variance typically grows with their mean (heteroscedastic in a specific, predictable way), and their distribution is naturally discrete and right-skewed for low counts. The Poisson GLM exists to model exactly this kind of data correctly — guaranteeing positive predictions, encoding the natural mean-variance relationship, and providing coefficients with a clean multiplicative interpretation directly relevant to demand and operations forecasting.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.how_it_works: Assumes Y | X ~ Poisson(μ), where log(μ) = Xβ (canonical log link) — so μ = exp(Xβ), guaranteeing positive expected counts for any input. The Poisson distribution's defining property — variance equals mean (Var(Y) = E[Y] = μ) — means the model automatically encodes 'larger expected counts come with proportionally larger variability,' a pattern real count data usually shows. Coefficients have a multiplicative interpretation: e^β represents the multiplicative change in expected count per one-unit increase in the predictor (e.g., e^β = 1.15 means 'a 15% increase in expected demand'). Fitting uses Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS, see [[Fitting via IRLS (iteratively reweighted least squares)]]); model fit/calibration is checked via deviance residuals and goodness-of-fit tests rather than raw R².
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.use_when: Use for genuinely count-valued targets where the Poisson's variance=mean assumption is roughly appropriate — moderate-volume demand forecasting, event-rate modeling, low-to-moderate-frequency occurrence data — and where you want guaranteed-positive, naturally-interpretable (multiplicative) predictions.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.avoid_when: Avoid when your count data is *overdispersed* (variance noticeably exceeds the mean — extremely common in real-world counts due to unmodeled heterogeneity, clustering, or excess zeros) — Negative Binomial regression handles this more honestly. Avoid when zero-counts are far more frequent than the Poisson distribution would predict (e.g., many customers buy zero units in a given period for reasons distinct from 'low underlying demand') — zero-inflated or hurdle models are designed for that structure.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_goes_wrong: The single most common Poisson-GLM mistake: fitting it on overdispersed data without checking — the point predictions can look fine, but standard errors and prediction intervals come out far too narrow (because the model assumes variance = mean, when the true variance is, say, 3x the mean), producing dangerously overconfident uncertainty estimates that downstream decisions (safety stock levels, staffing) rely on. A standard diagnostic — comparing the residual deviance to its degrees of freedom (should be ≈1 under correct Poisson specification; values ≫1 signal overdispersion) — is often skipped, letting this issue go unnoticed until real-world forecast intervals prove far too narrow.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.real_example: A retail demand-forecasting team fit a Poisson GLM on daily unit sales and used its predicted intervals to set safety-stock levels. Stockouts occurred far more often than the model's '95% confidence' intervals implied. A dispersion check revealed the residual deviance was roughly 4x the degrees of freedom — substantial overdispersion driven by unmodeled store-to-store and day-to-day heterogeneity. Switching to a Negative Binomial GLM (same log link, same multiplicative coefficient interpretation, but with an extra dispersion parameter that decoupled variance from the mean) produced intervals that were appropriately wider — and far better calibrated against actual stockout rates — without sacrificing point-forecast accuracy.

2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_it_is: A Generalized Linear Model for modeling strictly-positive, continuous, right-skewed targets — invoice amounts, insurance claim sizes, call-center handling times, rainfall amounts — using the Gamma distribution (whose variance is proportional to the *square* of its mean) typically paired with a log link, fit via `statsmodels.GLM(family=sm.families.Gamma(link=sm.families.links.log()))` or `sklearn.linear_model.GammaRegressor`.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.why_it_exists: Many continuous business and scientific quantities are strictly positive and right-skewed (a few very large values, many small-to-moderate ones) — modeling them with ordinary linear regression risks predicting impossible negative values and mishandles their characteristic 'larger values are more variable, in a multiplicative sense' pattern. The Gamma GLM exists to model this specific, common shape correctly — guaranteeing positivity, encoding a realistic mean-variance relationship (constant *coefficient of variation*, i.e., relative variability stays roughly constant as the mean changes), and yielding naturally interpretable multiplicative coefficients.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.how_it_works: Assumes Y | X ~ Gamma(μ, ν), where (with a log link) log(μ) = Xβ, so μ = exp(Xβ) > 0 always. The Gamma distribution's defining mean-variance relationship is Var(Y) = μ²/ν — variance scales with the *square* of the mean, which is equivalent to saying the *coefficient of variation* (std/mean) is roughly constant — a pattern that fits many real positive-skewed quantities remarkably well (a $10 invoice and a $10,000 invoice both tend to have roughly proportional, not absolute, variability around their typical values). As with Poisson, the log link gives coefficients a multiplicative interpretation (e^β = multiplicative effect on the expected value). The shape parameter ν is estimated alongside the regression coefficients and governs the distribution's overall skewness.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.use_when: Use for strictly-positive continuous targets with right-skewed, multiplicatively-varying behavior — costs, durations, claim amounts, prices — especially when you want guaranteed-positive predictions and naturally multiplicative ('this factor increases expected cost by X%') coefficient interpretations that map cleanly onto business reasoning about percentage effects.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.avoid_when: Avoid when the target can be exactly zero with non-negligible frequency (the Gamma distribution has zero density at y=0 — a 'two-part' or Tweedie model that explicitly handles a probability mass at zero plus a continuous positive component is more appropriate, common in insurance claims where many policies have zero claims). Avoid when the target's variability doesn't actually scale with the square of its mean (check via diagnostic plots — a different family or a transformed-target linear model might fit better).
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_goes_wrong: Forcing Gamma-GLM machinery onto data with a substantial mass of exact zeros (common in claims, usage, and spend data — 'most customers had zero claims this month') produces a poorly-fitting model, since the Gamma distribution structurally cannot represent a probability spike at zero — Tweedie or hurdle/two-part models are the correct tools there. Log-transforming the target and fitting ordinary linear regression is sometimes used as a 'simpler' substitute for a Gamma GLM with a log link — but the two are *not* equivalent (they make different distributional assumptions about the error structure and produce systematically different point predictions after back-transformation, a subtlety that trips up many practitioners who assume 'log then OLS' is a drop-in replacement for the GLM).
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.real_example: An insurance team modeling claim severity (amount, given that a claim occurred — i.e., conditional on being positive) found that log-transforming the amount and fitting OLS produced systematically biased back-transformed predictions (a well-known issue — Jensen's inequality means E[exp(log Y)] ≠ E[Y] without a correction factor that's easy to get wrong). Switching directly to a Gamma GLM with a log link modeled the original-scale amounts directly, avoided the back-transformation bias entirely, and produced coefficients the actuarial team could interpret directly as 'this risk factor increases expected claim severity by X%' — a framing that matched how they already communicated risk to underwriters.

2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_it_is: A Generalized Linear Model for count data that generalizes the Poisson model by adding a separate dispersion parameter, allowing variance to exceed the mean (overdispersion) — Var(Y) = μ + αμ² for dispersion parameter α > 0 (reducing exactly to the Poisson model when α → 0) — fit via `statsmodels.GLM(family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial())` or `statsmodels.discrete.discrete_model.NegativeBinomial`.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.why_it_exists: Real-world count data is overdispersed far more often than not — the Poisson model's rigid assumption that variance equals the mean is a special case that rarely holds exactly once you account for unmodeled heterogeneity (different customers, locations, or time periods having systematically different baseline rates that the model's predictors don't fully capture). Negative Binomial regression exists to relax that rigid assumption — adding one extra parameter that lets the data determine how much 'extra' variability exists beyond what the mean alone would predict, producing far better-calibrated uncertainty estimates.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.how_it_works: Can be derived as a Poisson-Gamma mixture: imagine each observation's true rate λᵢ is itself drawn from a Gamma distribution (capturing unobserved heterogeneity across observations), and conditional on λᵢ, the count is Poisson(λᵢ) — marginalizing over this latent heterogeneity produces the Negative Binomial distribution, with its characteristic Var(Y) = μ + αμ² relationship (extra variance beyond the Poisson baseline μ, scaling with the square of the mean via α). As α → 0, this reduces exactly to the Poisson model — making Negative Binomial a strict generalization, never a worse fit (in terms of likelihood) than Poisson on the same data, and a likelihood-ratio test directly compares the two to determine whether the added dispersion parameter is statistically justified. Coefficients retain the same log-link multiplicative interpretation as Poisson regression.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.use_when: Use as the *default*, more-robust choice for count regression whenever you suspect (or haven't yet ruled out) overdispersion — which, in practice, is most of the time for real-world count data; it costs little (one extra parameter) and protects against the common, consequential failure of underestimated uncertainty that plain Poisson models exhibit on overdispersed data.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.avoid_when: If a formal dispersion check (residual deviance / degrees of freedom ≈ 1, or a likelihood-ratio test against the nested Poisson model) confirms no meaningful overdispersion, the simpler Poisson model is perfectly adequate and slightly easier to fit, interpret, and explain — though there's rarely much cost to using Negative Binomial as a safe default and confirming α is small.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_goes_wrong: Conflating *overdispersion* (variance > mean due to unmodeled heterogeneity) with *zero-inflation* (more zeros than any standard count model predicts, often due to a structurally distinct 'never going to happen' subpopulation) — they look superficially similar in diagnostic plots but require different model families (Negative Binomial vs. zero-inflated/hurdle models) to fix correctly; misdiagnosing one as the other leaves the real problem unaddressed. Reporting the dispersion parameter α without explaining what it represents to non-technical stakeholders can make an otherwise-clear model presentation confusing — translating it into 'how much more variable real outcomes are than a naive count model would suggest' helps bridge that gap.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.real_example: Continuing the retail-demand example: after switching from Poisson to Negative Binomial regression, the team ran a likelihood-ratio test confirming the dispersion parameter α was statistically significant and substantial (α ≈ 0.6) — strong evidence the simpler Poisson model had been systematically wrong about uncertainty, not just slightly imprecise. The corrected model's wider, better-calibrated prediction intervals directly informed a revised safety-stock policy that cut both stockout incidents and excess-inventory carrying costs — a rare case where 'the uncertainty estimate was wrong' translated into a concrete, quantifiable operational fix.

2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_it_is: The standard estimation algorithm for fitting Generalized Linear Models — Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares solves the (generally nonlinear, non-closed-form) GLM maximum-likelihood problem by repeatedly solving a *weighted* linear-regression problem, where the weights and 'working response' are updated at each iteration based on the current parameter estimates, until convergence.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.why_it_exists: Unlike ordinary linear regression (which has a direct closed-form solution via the normal equations), most GLMs — Poisson, logistic, Gamma regression — have no closed-form maximum-likelihood solution because their link functions are nonlinear. IRLS exists as an elegant general-purpose solution: it reduces the hard nonlinear optimization problem to a *sequence* of easy linear-regression problems, each solvable via the well-understood weighted-least-squares machinery, converging to the maximum-likelihood estimate — turning an intractable-looking problem into a repeated application of a tractable one.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.how_it_works: Starting from an initial guess for β, each iteration: (1) compute the current linear predictor η = Xβ and fitted mean μ = g⁻¹(η); (2) form a 'working response' z = η + (y − μ)·g'(μ) (a linearized approximation of the link-transformed response around the current estimate); (3) compute weights w = 1/[g'(μ)²·V(μ)] (where V(μ) is the distribution's mean-variance function — e.g., V(μ)=μ for Poisson, V(μ)=μ² for Gamma — directly connecting back to the exponential-family structure); (4) solve the weighted least-squares problem β_new = (XᵀWX)⁻¹XᵀWz; (5) repeat until β converges. This is mathematically equivalent to Fisher scoring (Newton-Raphson using the expected, rather than observed, Hessian/information matrix) — a connection that explains both its convergence properties and why it naturally produces the standard errors GLM software reports.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.use_when: You don't typically invoke IRLS directly — `statsmodels.GLM.fit()` and equivalent library functions run it under the hood. Understanding it helps you interpret convergence warnings (non-convergence often signals separation, extreme outliers, or a poorly-specified model), understand why GLM fitting is iterative (and thus can fail to converge, unlike OLS's guaranteed one-shot solution), and appreciate why GLM standard errors come 'for free' from the same machinery that estimates the coefficients.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.avoid_when: Not a tool you choose to use or avoid — it's the estimation engine beneath GLM fitting. The relevant judgment call is whether to trust default convergence settings (tolerance, max iterations) or investigate further when fitting is slow, unstable, or produces convergence warnings.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.what_goes_wrong: Convergence failures or warnings are common symptoms of deeper data problems — e.g., 'perfect separation' in logistic regression (a predictor perfectly distinguishes the two classes, driving coefficient estimates toward infinity and IRLS toward non-convergence), extreme outliers that destabilize the iterative weighting scheme, or a fundamentally misspecified link/family combination. Practitioners sometimes respond to convergence warnings by simply increasing `max_iter` and moving on — masking a real underlying data or specification issue rather than diagnosing and fixing it. Because the weights `w` depend on the *current* fitted values, a poor starting point or pathological data can cause the iteration to oscillate or diverge rather than smoothly converge — a failure mode that OLS's one-shot closed-form solution simply cannot exhibit.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Generalised.real_example: A logistic-regression GLM fit on fraud-detection data threw repeated convergence warnings; investigation revealed 'perfect separation' — a single binary feature (`account_flagged_by_partner_bank`) was true for 100% of fraud cases and false for 100% of legitimate ones in the training sample (a data-leakage artifact from how the training set had been assembled). IRLS was correctly trying to push that coefficient toward infinity because the data, as given, supported an infinitely confident rule — the 'failure to converge' was the algorithm correctly reporting a real, serious problem with the training data, not a numerical glitch to be silenced with a higher iteration limit.

2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.what_it_is: A regression adaptation of Support Vector Machines that fits a function within an ε-wide 'tube' around the predicted values, ignoring (treating as zero loss) any training errors smaller than ε and penalizing only points that fall outside the tube — producing a sparse, margin-based regression model defined by a subset of 'support vectors.'
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.why_it_exists: Ordinary least-squares regression penalizes every deviation from the fitted line, however small, and is sensitive to the exact noise in every training point. SVR exists to encode a different, often more robust philosophy: 'don't worry about errors smaller than some tolerance ε — only points that genuinely violate that tolerance should influence the fit.' This produces models that are less sensitive to small perturbations in the data and, via the kernel trick, can capture nonlinear relationships with the same elegant margin-based theory that makes SVMs powerful for classification.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.how_it_works: SVR minimizes (1/2)||w||² + C·Σ(ξᵢ + ξᵢ*), subject to the constraint that predictions fall within ε of the true values (with slack variables ξ, ξ* allowing controlled violations) — the ε-insensitive loss function is exactly zero for |y − ŷ| ≤ ε and grows linearly beyond that. Only points outside the ε-tube ('support vectors') contribute to the final model — points well-fit within the tube are effectively ignored, producing a typically sparse solution. The regularization parameter C trades off margin width against tolerance for tube violations (low C → wider tolerance for violations, simpler model; high C → less tolerance, more complex fit). As with SVM classification, the kernel trick (RBF, polynomial kernels) lets SVR capture nonlinear relationships by implicitly operating in a higher-dimensional feature space without ever computing it explicitly.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.use_when: Use for small-to-medium datasets with potentially nonlinear relationships where robustness to small-noise perturbations matters and you want a principled, margin-based alternative to tree ensembles — common in scientific/engineering domains with smooth underlying physical relationships and modest data volumes.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.avoid_when: Avoid for large datasets — SVR's training cost scales poorly (roughly quadratic-to-cubic in the number of samples for kernel methods), making it impractical at scale where tree ensembles or neural networks dominate both in speed and typically in accuracy. Avoid when features aren't scaled — SVR (like all kernel/distance-based methods) is highly sensitive to feature scale, and unscaled inputs can produce a badly-fit, seemingly-arbitrary model.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to scale features before fitting causes the kernel's distance computations to be dominated by large-scale features, producing poor fits that look like 'the algorithm doesn't work' rather than 'the inputs weren't prepared correctly.' Choosing ε too large makes the model insensitive to genuine signal (everything falls 'within tolerance,' producing an underfit, nearly-flat model); choosing it too small effectively reverts to ordinary squared-error-like sensitivity, losing SVR's robustness benefit. The three interacting hyperparameters (C, ε, and kernel parameters like RBF's γ) create a search space that's easy to under-tune, leading to disappointing performance that's actually a tuning problem, not a fundamental limitation of the method.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.real_example: A team modeling a sensor calibration curve (smooth, mildly nonlinear, with known measurement noise of roughly ±0.5 units) used SVR with an RBF kernel and ε set to match the known noise floor (0.5) — explicitly telling the model 'don't chase noise smaller than the sensor's own precision.' This produced a smoother, more physically-plausible fit than a tree ensemble (which chased every small fluctuation, including ones the team knew were pure measurement noise) — a case where domain knowledge about the noise floor mapped directly and naturally onto SVR's central hyperparameter, a fit between method and problem that doesn't arise as cleanly with most other regressors.

2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.what_it_is: A non-parametric regression method that predicts a new point's target value as the (optionally distance-weighted) average of the target values of its K nearest neighbors in feature space — `sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor` — making no assumptions about the functional form of the relationship between features and target.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.why_it_exists: Many relationships don't follow any simple parametric form (linear, polynomial, exponential) — they're just 'similar inputs tend to have similar outputs,' a purely local, non-parametric notion of structure. KNN regression exists to operationalize that intuition directly: rather than fitting global parameters, it makes each prediction by looking at what happened to similar examples nearby — a simple, interpretable, assumption-light baseline that can capture arbitrarily complex local structure given enough data.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.how_it_works: For a new point x, find the K training points closest to x (by a distance metric — Euclidean by default, though others can be specified), and predict ŷ = mean(y of K neighbors) for uniform weighting, or a distance-weighted average (`weights='distance'`) where closer neighbors contribute more — useful when neighbor distances vary meaningfully. K controls the bias-variance trade-off directly: small K (e.g., K=1) produces a highly flexible, low-bias, high-variance model that can overfit to local noise; large K produces a smoother, higher-bias, lower-variance model that can underfit and blur over genuine local structure. There is no 'training' in the usual sense — the entire training set is stored, and computation happens at prediction time (a 'lazy learner'), which is why distance computation cost (and thus prediction-time latency) scales with training-set size unless accelerated by spatial index structures (KD-trees, ball trees).
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.use_when: Use as a simple, interpretable, assumption-free baseline for small-to-medium, low-to-moderate-dimensional datasets where you suspect 'local similarity' genuinely drives the target, and where prediction-time latency from storing/searching the full training set is acceptable.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.avoid_when: Avoid in high-dimensional feature spaces — the 'curse of dimensionality' means that in high dimensions, all points tend to become roughly equidistant from each other, and the notion of 'nearest neighbor' loses its discriminative meaning (distances stop being informative). Avoid for large datasets with latency-sensitive serving requirements — the lazy-learning, store-everything approach makes prediction cost scale with training-set size, unlike eagerly-trained parametric or tree-based models whose prediction cost is independent of training-set size.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to scale features causes distance calculations to be dominated by large-scale features — exactly the same trap as with SVR and any other distance-based method, and arguably even more consequential here since the *entire* prediction mechanism is distance-based. Choosing K via a single validation check rather than cross-validation can land on an unstable value; K is frequently the single most important hyperparameter and deserves a proper sweep. In high dimensions, KNN regression can silently degrade into something close to 'predict the global mean' — because all neighbor distances become similar, the 'nearest' neighbors aren't meaningfully more similar than random points — a failure mode that's easy to miss without explicitly checking how informative distances actually are in your feature space.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.real_example: A team building a house-price estimator used raw features including `square_footage` (range: hundreds to thousands) and `num_bathrooms` (range: 1-5) directly in KNN regression — distance calculations were entirely dominated by square footage, so 'nearest neighbors' were essentially just 'houses of similar size,' ignoring bathroom count, location, and other features almost completely. Standardizing all features before fitting (`StandardScaler` in a `Pipeline`) produced neighbors that were genuinely similar across *all* dimensions, immediately improving cross-validated MAE by 18% — a fix that took one line of code once the underlying distance-scale issue was correctly diagnosed.

2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.what_it_is: A tree-based regression model (CART — Classification And Regression Trees, for the regression case) that recursively partitions the feature space into rectangular regions by choosing, at each node, the feature and threshold that most reduces the variance (mean squared error) of the target within the resulting child nodes — predicting, for any new input, the average target value of the training examples in the leaf it falls into.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.why_it_exists: Linear models assume additive, globally-linear relationships; KNN makes purely local, distance-based predictions that struggle in high dimensions. Decision trees exist to offer a third path: a model that can represent arbitrarily complex, nonlinear, *interaction-rich* relationships (the effect of one feature can depend entirely on the value of another) through a sequence of simple, human-readable if/else rules — directly interpretable, requiring no feature scaling, and serving as the foundational building block for the powerful ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) that dominate tabular ML.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.how_it_works: Starting from the root (containing all training data), the algorithm searches over all features and all possible split thresholds, selecting the (feature, threshold) pair that most reduces the weighted variance (MSE) of the target across the two resulting child nodes — `Var_reduction = Var(parent) − [w_left·Var(left) + w_right·Var(right)]`. This process recurses on each child node, continuing until a stopping criterion is met (`max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, `min_samples_split`, or no further reduction is possible). A new point's prediction is the mean target value of all training examples that landed in the same leaf — effectively a piecewise-constant approximation of the true function, with the 'pieces' (regions) chosen adaptively to minimize within-region variance.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.use_when: Use as an interpretable baseline that requires no feature scaling and naturally handles nonlinearity and feature interactions, or — far more commonly in practice — as the base learner inside ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost) that combine many trees to dramatically improve on a single tree's accuracy and stability.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.avoid_when: Avoid relying on a single decision tree for production-grade predictive performance — they're notoriously high-variance (small data perturbations can produce structurally very different trees) and prone to overfitting without careful pruning/regularization; ensembles consistently outperform single trees on tabular data. Avoid for problems requiring smooth, continuous predictions — a tree's piecewise-constant output produces visible 'step' discontinuities that can look unnatural for inherently smooth physical or economic relationships.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.what_goes_wrong: An unconstrained tree (`max_depth=None`) will grow until every leaf is pure (or nearly so), perfectly memorizing the training data — spectacular training R² and dismal validation performance, the canonical decision-tree overfitting pattern. Small changes in the training data (a handful of added/removed rows) can produce dramatically different tree structures — the high-variance instability that directly motivated the invention of bagging (Random Forest) as a remedy. The piecewise-constant prediction surface means a tree can never extrapolate beyond the range of values it saw during training — for any input outside the training range, it simply returns the prediction of whichever boundary leaf the input falls into, which can be badly wrong for genuinely out-of-range inputs.

The general workflow: train the base model on one portion of data, fit the calibration mapping on a separate held-out portion (`sklearn.calibration.CalibratedClassifierCV` automates this with cross-validation), and evaluate calibration quality via reliability diagrams / calibration curves (plotting predicted vs. observed frequencies) and proper scoring rules (Brier score, log loss) that reward both good ranking *and* good calibration.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.use_when: Use whenever a model's raw output values feed directly into decisions that depend on their absolute meaning — risk scoring (e.g., 'is this loan-default probability of 0.3 *actually* a 30% chance?'), medical risk stratification, expected-value/cost-benefit calculations, or any pipeline where a downstream system treats the score as a literal probability or expected quantity rather than just a ranking signal.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.avoid_when: Avoid spending calibration effort when only *ranking* matters (e.g., 'show the top-10 most-likely-to-churn customers,' where the absolute scores never surface to a decision-maker) — calibration changes the absolute meaning of scores without improving (and sometimes slightly degrading) their rank-ordering, so it's pure overhead for rank-only use cases. Avoid isotonic regression specifically when the calibration set is small — its flexibility becomes a liability, fitting noise in the small calibration sample rather than the true miscalibration pattern; Platt scaling's more constrained sigmoid form is the safer choice in low-data calibration regimes.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.what_goes_wrong: Fitting the calibration mapping on the *same* data used to train the base model causes the calibration step to 'correct for' overfitting patterns that won't generalize — producing a mapping that looks good on training data and fails on genuinely new data; calibration absolutely requires a separate held-out set, just like the base model's own validation. Evaluating only discrimination metrics (AUC, accuracy) before and after calibration can mask the real story — calibration is specifically designed to improve *calibration* quality (Brier score, log loss, reliability diagrams), often while leaving discrimination metrics essentially unchanged (since monotonic recalibration doesn't change rank order); judging calibration's success by the wrong metric leads to the false conclusion that 'it didn't do anything.' Choosing isotonic regression by default 'because it's more flexible' without checking calibration-set size is a common trap — its flexibility is a double-edged sword that requires enough data to wield safely; Platt scaling is frequently the more robust real-world choice specifically because it assumes less and therefore needs less data to do so safely.
2|🔴 T1 Regression Algorithms|Other Regre.real_example: A lending-risk team's gradient boosting model achieved excellent AUC (0.91) for ranking applicants by default risk, but when the business team began using the model's raw scores directly as 'probability of default' inputs to expected-loss calculations, actual default rates among applicants scored '0.2' were closer to 0.35 — a serious, costly miscalibration that AUC alone had completely hidden (since AUC only cares about ranking, not absolute values). Applying Platt scaling on a held-out calibration set (chosen over isotonic regression because the calibration set was modest in size — about 8,000 examples) brought predicted-vs-observed default rates into close alignment across all score deciles (verified via a reliability diagram and a Brier-score improvement from 0.19 to 0.11), while AUC remained essentially unchanged at 0.91 — exactly the expected signature of a successful calibration fix: rankings preserved, absolute meaning repaired.

2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.what_it_is: A linear model for classification that applies the sigmoid function (binary case) or softmax function (multiclass case) to a linear combination of input features, producing class probabilities, and is trained by minimizing log-loss (cross-entropy) — `sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` — one of the most widely used, interpretable, and well-understood classification algorithms.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.why_it_exists: Linear regression's outputs are unbounded real numbers, but classification requires probabilities (bounded in [0,1]) that sum to one across classes. Logistic regression exists to bridge that gap elegantly: by passing a linear score through the sigmoid (which squashes any real number into (0,1)) or softmax (which generalizes this to multiple classes while preserving a valid probability distribution), it retains the simplicity, speed, and interpretability of a linear model while producing outputs that are *directly usable* as probabilities — making it the natural, principled starting point for nearly any classification problem.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.how_it_works: Compute a linear score z = w·x + b, then apply σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(-z)) to map it to a probability P(y=1|x) ∈ (0,1) for binary classification, or apply softmax(z)ᵢ = e^(zᵢ)/Σⱼe^(zⱼ) across C linear scores to produce a valid probability distribution over C classes. Training minimizes log-loss (cross-entropy): L = −Σ[yᵢ·log(p̂ᵢ) + (1−yᵢ)·log(1−p̂ᵢ)] for binary, or its multiclass generalization — a convex objective with a unique global minimum, solvable efficiently via gradient-based optimizers (L-BFGS, SAG, SAGA, or plain gradient descent for large-scale variants). The decision boundary in input space is linear (a hyperplane) — the sigmoid/softmax transformation reshapes the *output* into a probability, but the underlying boundary between classes remains exactly as linear as in linear regression, which is both the model's defining simplicity and its fundamental limitation. Regularization (L1/L2/elasticnet, controlled by `C` — note: inverse of regularization strength) is built directly into the standard implementation, helping prevent overfitting and, in the L1 case, inducing sparsity (automatic feature selection).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.use_when: Use as the default first model for any classification problem — it's fast to train, easy to interpret (coefficients show feature direction and rough magnitude of effect on log-odds), provides well-calibrated probability estimates out of the box, and serves as a strong baseline that more complex models must justify beating.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.avoid_when: Avoid when the true decision boundary between classes is substantially nonlinear — logistic regression cannot represent curved or complex boundaries without explicit feature engineering (polynomial features, interaction terms) or kernelization, at which point tree ensembles or other nonlinear methods often serve the purpose more directly and with less manual effort.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to scale features before applying L1/L2 regularization causes the penalty to act unevenly across features of different scales — large-scale features get penalized less relative to their coefficient magnitudes, distorting which features the regularization 'chooses' to shrink, an easily-overlooked but consequential preprocessing omission. Interpreting coefficients as if they were on the *probability* scale rather than the *log-odds* scale leads to systematically wrong conclusions — a coefficient of 0.5 doesn't mean 'increases probability by 50%,' it means 'increases log-odds by 0.5,' a distinction that matters enormously when communicating results to non-technical stakeholders. Using the default `C` (regularization strength) without tuning via cross-validation can leave significant performance on the table in either direction — too little regularization overfits on noisy/high-dimensional data, too much underfits and discards genuine signal.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.real_example: A team explaining a credit-approval model's logistic regression coefficients to a compliance team initially said 'a $10K income increase raises approval probability by 0.3' — directly reading the coefficient as a probability change. After realizing the coefficient (0.3) was actually a log-odds effect, they instead reported it correctly as 'multiplies the odds of approval by e^0.3 ≈ 1.35' and additionally computed the *marginal effect* at the average applicant's profile (using `predict_proba` derivatives) to give compliance officers an intuitive 'roughly +6 percentage points at a typical applicant's income level' — illustrating that getting real value from logistic regression's interpretability requires correctly translating between the log-odds scale the model operates on and the probability scale humans actually reason in.

2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.what_it_is: A generative classification method that models each class's feature distribution as a multivariate Gaussian sharing a *common* covariance matrix across all classes, then classifies new points by which class's Gaussian assigns them the highest posterior probability (via Bayes' theorem) — `sklearn.discriminant_analysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis` — producing linear decision boundaries as a direct mathematical consequence of the shared-covariance assumption.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.why_it_exists: Logistic regression directly models the decision boundary (discriminative approach) without describing how the data within each class is distributed. LDA exists to take the opposite, *generative* path: explicitly model how each class generates its features (as a Gaussian), then derive the optimal classification rule from those generative models via Bayes' theorem — an approach that, when its Gaussian and shared-covariance assumptions hold reasonably well, can be more statistically efficient (better performance with less data) than discriminative methods, and additionally provides a natural route to dimensionality reduction (LDA can project data onto the directions that best separate classes).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.how_it_works: Estimate each class's mean vector μ_c and a single *pooled* (shared) covariance matrix Σ from the training data; classify a new point x by computing, for each class, the discriminant function δ_c(x) = x^T Σ⁻¹ μ_c − ½μ_c^T Σ⁻¹ μ_c + log(P(class=c)), and predicting the class with the highest value. Because all classes share the same Σ, the quadratic terms involving Σ cancel out when comparing classes, leaving a function that's *linear* in x — this is precisely why LDA produces linear decision boundaries (the 'L' in LDA), a direct mathematical consequence of the shared-covariance assumption rather than an externally-imposed constraint. Beyond classification, the directions that maximize between-class separation relative to within-class scatter (the LDA 'components') can be used for supervised dimensionality reduction — projecting high-dimensional data onto at most C−1 dimensions (C = number of classes) while preserving maximal class-discriminative information, useful both for visualization and as a preprocessing step.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.use_when: Use when class distributions are roughly Gaussian with similar covariance structure (or when you specifically want the supervised-dimensionality-reduction capability that LDA's projection directions provide), and when training data is limited — LDA's stronger generative assumptions let it estimate good decision boundaries from less data than purely discriminative methods sometimes need.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.avoid_when: Avoid when class covariance structures genuinely differ substantially — forcing a shared-covariance assumption onto data that doesn't satisfy it produces systematically suboptimal (and sometimes badly wrong) decision boundaries; QDA (which allows per-class covariances) is the natural escalation when this assumption is violated. Avoid when feature distributions are visibly non-Gaussian (heavily skewed, multimodal, with heavy outliers) — LDA's performance degrades as the Gaussian assumption is increasingly violated, and tree-based or kernel methods that make no distributional assumptions become more appropriate.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.what_goes_wrong: Applying LDA to data with substantially different per-class covariances (e.g., one class tightly clustered, another widely dispersed) produces a linear boundary that's a poor compromise between what each class's *true* optimal (curved) boundary would look like — performance suffers in a way that's easy to misdiagnose as 'the data is just hard' rather than 'the shared-covariance assumption doesn't fit.' Not checking whether features are approximately Gaussian (via Q-Q plots, Shapiro-Wilk tests, or simple histograms) before applying LDA risks building on an invalid foundation — a quick exploratory check that's often skipped in the rush to get a baseline running. Confusing LDA-as-classifier with LDA-as-dimensionality-reduction-tool can lead to using it for one purpose while implicitly relying on assumptions only justified for the other — e.g., using its projections for visualization without realizing the projection itself optimizes for class separation (a supervised criterion), which can mislead if mistaken for an unsupervised technique like PCA.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.real_example: A team comparing LDA and QDA on a three-class material-classification problem found LDA achieved 81% accuracy while QDA achieved 89% — investigating why revealed that one material class had nearly triple the feature variance of the other two (a genuinely heteroscedastic structure that violated LDA's shared-covariance assumption). Rather than simply adopting QDA wholesale, the team used the comparison itself as a diagnostic — the LDA-vs-QDA accuracy gap became a quick, principled way to detect and quantify covariance heterogeneity across classes, informing decisions about feature engineering (could the high-variance class's features be transformed to better match the others?) well beyond just picking the better-performing model.

2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.what_it_is: A generative classification method closely related to LDA that models each class's features as a multivariate Gaussian, but — unlike LDA — allows each class to have its *own* covariance matrix, producing quadratic (curved) decision boundaries — `sklearn.discriminant_analysis.QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis` — trading LDA's simplicity and lower variance for greater flexibility in representing differently-shaped class distributions.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.why_it_exists: LDA's shared-covariance assumption is a strong constraint that, when violated, produces systematically suboptimal linear boundaries no matter how much data you provide. QDA exists as the natural relaxation: by letting each class have its own covariance structure, it can represent decision boundaries that curve to match the actual shapes of differently-distributed classes — capturing more of the true structure when that structure genuinely varies by class, at the cost of needing more parameters (and thus more data) to estimate those per-class covariances reliably.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.how_it_works: Estimate a separate mean vector μ_c *and* a separate covariance matrix Σ_c for each class; classify a new point by computing each class's discriminant function (now retaining the quadratic terms that canceled in LDA, since Σ_c differs across classes) and predicting the class with the highest value — δ_c(x) = −½log|Σ_c| − ½(x−μ_c)^T Σ_c⁻¹(x−μ_c) + log(P(class=c)). Because the quadratic term (x−μ_c)^T Σ_c⁻¹(x−μ_c) no longer cancels between classes (each has its own Σ_c), the resulting decision boundary is genuinely quadratic — curves, ellipses, parabolas — capable of representing relationships LDA structurally cannot. The cost: each class's covariance matrix has O(p²) parameters to estimate (p = number of features) — for high-dimensional data or classes with few examples, these estimates become noisy and unstable, a direct manifestation of the bias-variance trade-off (QDA trades LDA's higher bias for higher variance).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.use_when: Use when you have reasonable evidence (via exploratory analysis or an LDA-vs-QDA comparison) that class covariance structures genuinely differ, and you have enough data per class to estimate each covariance matrix reliably — QDA's added flexibility pays off precisely when the extra parameters can be estimated with confidence.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.avoid_when: Avoid in high-dimensional settings with limited data — the number of covariance parameters to estimate grows quadratically with feature count, and with few examples per class, those estimates become unreliable, leading to unstable, overfit decision boundaries; this is a textbook bias-variance trade-off where QDA's lower bias is overwhelmed by its higher variance. Avoid when classes have similar covariance structure (then LDA's simpler, lower-variance model will likely generalize better with the same data) — always worth checking via a direct LDA-vs-QDA comparison before committing to the more complex model.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.what_goes_wrong: Applying QDA to a dataset with many features but few examples per class produces covariance matrix estimates dominated by sampling noise — the model can achieve excellent training accuracy (fitting noise-driven curved boundaries) while generalizing poorly, a classic high-variance overfitting signature that's easy to misattribute to 'the problem is just hard.' Not comparing against the simpler LDA baseline risks adopting unnecessary complexity — if LDA performs comparably, its lower-variance linear boundaries will likely generalize better on new data, and the added quadratic flexibility was solving a problem that didn't exist. Forgetting that QDA, like LDA, assumes Gaussian class-conditional distributions means that genuinely non-Gaussian data (multimodal classes, heavy skew) will be poorly served by *either* method — the LDA-vs-QDA choice only matters once the more fundamental Gaussian assumption is reasonably satisfied.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.real_example: A team applying QDA to a 50-feature medical diagnosis dataset with only ~40 examples per class found training accuracy of 98% but cross-validated accuracy of just 64% — a huge gap traced to covariance matrices each requiring estimation of 50×51/2 ≈ 1,275 parameters from a mere 40 data points per class, producing wildly noisy, overfit estimates. Switching to LDA (which pools all classes' data to estimate a single shared covariance matrix, effectively using ~3× more data per parameter) raised cross-validated accuracy to 79% — a clear demonstration that QDA's extra flexibility is only an advantage when there's enough data to support it, and that 'more flexible model' and 'better model' are very much not synonyms.

2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.what_it_is: One of the earliest and simplest linear classification algorithms, which updates its weight vector incrementally — one training example at a time — by adding (or subtracting) the misclassified example's feature vector whenever a prediction is wrong, continuing until all examples are classified correctly or a maximum iteration count is reached — `sklearn.linear_model.Perceptron` — a foundational building block in the history of neural networks and online learning.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.why_it_exists: The perceptron exists historically as one of the first algorithms to demonstrate that a machine could *learn* a decision rule from labeled examples through simple, local, iterative corrections — directly inspired by (an early, simplified model of) biological neurons, and serving as the conceptual ancestor of modern neural networks (a single-layer perceptron is, in essence, one artificial neuron). Practically, it remains relevant as an extremely simple, fast, online-learning algorithm — useful when data arrives incrementally (streaming) and you need a model that updates example-by-example without retraining from scratch.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.how_it_works: Initialize weights w (often to zero); for each training example (xᵢ, yᵢ), compute the prediction ŷᵢ = sign(w·xᵢ); if the prediction is correct, do nothing — if it's wrong, update w ← w + η·yᵢ·xᵢ (nudging the weight vector in the direction that would have produced the correct prediction for this example), where η is the learning rate. Repeat over the dataset (potentially many passes/epochs) until either no examples are misclassified (the algorithm has converged) or a maximum iteration count is reached. The famous **Perceptron Convergence Theorem** guarantees that *if the data is linearly separable*, this process will converge to a separating hyperplane in a finite number of steps — but provides **no such guarantee if the data is not linearly separable**, in which case the algorithm can oscillate indefinitely, never settling on a final answer (a fundamental limitation that motivated the development of more robust methods like logistic regression and SVMs, which handle non-separable data gracefully via probabilistic framing or soft margins).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.use_when: Use for simple, fast, online/streaming classification tasks where data arrives incrementally and a lightweight, easily-updatable linear model suffices — or in educational/historical contexts to build intuition for how iterative, error-driven learning works as a precursor to modern neural network training.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.avoid_when: Avoid for production classification tasks requiring robust performance on non-linearly-separable data — the perceptron provides no convergence guarantee in that common case, and offers no probabilistic outputs, regularization, or soft-margin handling of noisy/overlapping classes that logistic regression and SVMs provide essentially for free.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.what_goes_wrong: Running the perceptron on non-linearly-separable data (the overwhelmingly common real-world case) without a maximum-iteration safeguard can cause it to loop indefinitely, oscillating between weight configurations that each misclassify a different subset of points — a direct, visible consequence of the algorithm's lack of convergence guarantee outside the separable case. Treating the perceptron's raw output (a sign/threshold decision) as if it provided meaningful confidence or probability information is a category error — unlike logistic regression's calibrated probabilities, the perceptron only ever produces a hard classification decision, with no notion of 'how confident' that decision is. Forgetting that the final weight vector depends on the *order* in which training examples are processed (and on the random initialization, if non-zero) means re-running the algorithm on shuffled data can produce a different — though equally 'correct' on separable data — final boundary, a source of surprising non-reproducibility for those expecting deterministic behavior from a simple linear model.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Linear.real_example: A team building an introductory ML course used the perceptron specifically to create a memorable 'aha' moment: they first ran it on a synthetic, perfectly linearly-separable two-class dataset (rapid, clean convergence to a perfect separator), then ran it — unchanged — on the same data with just 5% label noise added (making it non-separable). The algorithm visibly failed to converge, oscillating between different imperfect boundaries across epochs — a deliberately-staged contrast that made the abstract concept of 'no convergence guarantee on non-separable data' concrete and visceral, motivating *why* the next lecture's topic (logistic regression's probabilistic framing, which handles overlapping classes gracefully) represented genuine algorithmic progress rather than just 'a different way to draw a line.'

2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.what_it_is: A non-parametric classification method that predicts a new point's class by majority vote among its K nearest neighbors in feature space (by some distance metric) — `sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier` — making no assumptions about the functional form of the decision boundary, and instead letting 'what happened to similar examples' directly determine the prediction.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.why_it_exists: Many real-world decision boundaries don't follow any clean parametric form — they're irregular, locally-varying, shaped by complex interactions that no simple equation captures cleanly. KNN exists to sidestep the need to specify such a form altogether: it operationalizes the simple, intuitive idea that 'similar inputs should get similar labels' directly and non-parametrically, serving as a conceptually transparent baseline and a useful tool whenever 'local similarity' is plausibly the dominant structure in the data.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.how_it_works: For a new point x, identify the K training points closest to it by a chosen distance metric (Euclidean by default), then predict the class that appears most frequently among those K neighbors (optionally weighting votes by inverse distance, so closer neighbors count more). K directly controls the bias-variance trade-off: small K (e.g., K=1) yields a highly flexible decision boundary that can fit training data (including noise) almost perfectly — high variance, prone to overfitting; large K produces smoother, more conservative boundaries — higher bias, prone to underfitting and blurring genuine local structure (in the extreme, K = entire training set reduces to 'always predict the majority class'). The **curse of dimensionality** is KNN's central, defining vulnerability: as the number of features grows, the volume of feature space grows exponentially, data points become increasingly sparse relative to that volume, and — counterintuitively — the *distances* between any two points tend to converge toward similar values, so 'nearest' neighbors stop being meaningfully more similar than random points; the entire algorithm's foundational assumption (that proximity implies similarity) quietly erodes as dimensionality increases.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.use_when: Use as a simple, interpretable, assumption-free baseline for low-to-moderate-dimensional classification problems where local similarity plausibly drives class membership, and where you can tolerate prediction-time costs that scale with training-set size (it requires no explicit training phase — the data itself *is* the model).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.avoid_when: Avoid in high-dimensional feature spaces — the curse of dimensionality erodes the very notion of 'nearest,' often silently degrading KNN toward something close to random or majority-class prediction. Avoid when prediction-time latency matters and the training set is large — unlike eagerly-trained parametric models (logistic regression, trees), KNN must search the (potentially huge) stored training set at prediction time for every single query.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.what_goes_wrong: Applying KNN directly to high-dimensional data (hundreds of features) without dimensionality reduction (PCA, feature selection, embeddings) often yields disappointing, hard-to-diagnose performance — the model technically runs and produces predictions, but those predictions are barely better than chance because 'nearest neighbor' has lost its discriminative meaning, a failure mode that looks like 'the data has no signal' but is actually 'the distance metric has stopped being informative in this many dimensions.' Forgetting to scale features (the same trap that affects every distance-based method) lets large-scale features dominate the distance computation, silently ignoring smaller-scale but potentially more predictive ones. Choosing K via a single train/validation split rather than cross-validation risks landing on an unstable choice — K is frequently *the* most consequential hyperparameter, and a proper sweep with cross-validation is cheap insurance against a poor pick.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.real_example: A team built a KNN classifier on a customer dataset with 200 raw features (many sparse, one-hot-encoded categorical columns) and found accuracy barely above the majority-class baseline — investigation revealed that in 200 dimensions, the ratio of the nearest to farthest neighbor's distance for a typical query point was close to 1.0 (i.e., all points were nearly equidistant), confirming the curse of dimensionality had effectively destroyed the signal KNN depends on. Applying PCA to reduce to the top 15 components (capturing ~85% of variance) before running KNN raised accuracy from 52% to 74% — not because PCA added information, but because it concentrated the *existing* signal into a low-enough-dimensional space for 'nearest neighbor' to mean something again.

2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.what_it_is: Spatial indexing data structures — KD-trees (k-dimensional trees) and ball trees — that organize training data into hierarchical, space-partitioning structures enabling much faster nearest-neighbor lookups than brute-force distance computation against every training point, used internally by `sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier` (and regressor) via the `algorithm` parameter (`'kd_tree'`, `'ball_tree'`, `'brute'`, or `'auto'`).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.why_it_exists: Brute-force KNN search computes the distance from a query point to *every* training point — an O(n) operation per query that becomes prohibitively slow as training-set size grows. KD-trees and ball trees exist to make this dramatically faster by pre-organizing the data into a hierarchical structure that lets the search *prune* large swaths of the dataset — regions provably too far away to contain the nearest neighbors — without ever computing their distances explicitly, turning an O(n) search into something closer to O(log n) in favorable conditions.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.how_it_works: **KD-tree**: recursively partitions feature space along alternating coordinate axes (split on feature 1's median, then feature 2's median, and so on, cycling through dimensions), building a binary tree where each node represents an axis-aligned splitting hyperplane; nearest-neighbor search descends the tree toward the query point's region, then 'backtracks' to check sibling branches only if they could possibly contain a closer point than the best found so far (a provable geometric bound enables skipping branches that can't). **Ball tree**: instead of axis-aligned splits, partitions data into nested hyperspheres ('balls'), each defined by a center and radius — better suited to high-dimensional or non-uniformly-distributed data, where axis-aligned partitioning (KD-tree's approach) becomes progressively less effective. **The crucial caveat**: both structures' speed advantage *degrades* as dimensionality increases — in very high dimensions, the curse of dimensionality (the same phenomenon that erodes KNN's predictive value) also erodes these structures' ability to prune effectively, since 'most points end up roughly equidistant' means few branches can be confidently ruled out; beyond roughly 20-30 dimensions, brute-force search often becomes competitive with or faster than tree-based search, and `algorithm='auto'` heuristically picks the best option based on data characteristics.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.use_when: Use (or simply trust `algorithm='auto'`) when working with low-to-moderate-dimensional data and large training sets, where the speedup from spatial indexing meaningfully reduces prediction latency — the default automatic selection in scikit-learn handles this trade-off sensibly in most cases.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.avoid_when: Avoid manually forcing `'kd_tree'` or `'ball_tree'` in genuinely high-dimensional settings (tens to hundreds of features) — the indexing overhead can exceed brute-force search's cost without providing the expected speedup, since pruning becomes ineffective; in such regimes, `'brute'` (or, better, a dimensionality-reduction step before KNN entirely) often performs comparably or better.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.what_goes_wrong: Assuming spatial indexing structures provide a 'free' speedup regardless of dimensionality is a common misconception — past a certain dimensionality, their pruning advantage evaporates due to the same curse-of-dimensionality phenomenon that degrades KNN's predictive accuracy, and forcing their use can paradoxically slow things down relative to brute force. Manually selecting `algorithm='kd_tree'` or `'ball_tree'` without benchmarking against `'auto'`/`'brute'` on your actual data risks locking in a suboptimal choice based on intuition rather than measurement — a quick empirical comparison (`%timeit` across algorithm options) is cheap and removes the guesswork. Not recognizing that these structures speed up *lookup*, not the fundamental *predictive* limitations of KNN in high dimensions, can lead to mistakenly believing 'using a KD-tree' addresses the curse-of-dimensionality problem — it addresses a completely orthogonal concern (search speed, not search meaningfulness).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.real_example: A team serving KNN predictions in a low-latency API initially left `algorithm='auto'` and found p99 latency of 45ms on their 12-feature, 2-million-row dataset — investigating the auto-selected algorithm revealed scikit-learn had chosen a ball tree, appropriate for their moderate dimensionality and large dataset size. When a later project reused the same KNN configuration on a 180-feature embedding-based dataset, latency *increased* to 120ms despite a smaller training set — profiling revealed the ball tree's traversal overhead now exceeded its pruning benefit in the higher-dimensional space; explicitly setting `algorithm='brute'` (which uses vectorized batch distance computation) cut latency back to 38ms — a concrete illustration that the 'best' search algorithm is data-dependent, and that benchmarking beats assuming.

2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.what_it_is: The family of mathematical functions used to quantify 'how far apart' two points are in feature space — Euclidean (straight-line/L2 distance), Manhattan (grid/L1 distance), Minkowski (a generalization parameterized by p that includes both as special cases), and Cosine (angle-based similarity, ignoring magnitude) — the foundational choice underlying every distance-based algorithm (KNN, K-Means, hierarchical clustering, and more).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.why_it_exists: 'Distance' is not a single, universal concept — different notions of similarity are appropriate for different kinds of data and different real-world meanings of 'closeness.' This family of metrics exists to give practitioners principled options: Euclidean for genuine straight-line spatial relationships, Manhattan for grid-like or robustness-to-outlier scenarios, Minkowski as a tunable generalization spanning both, and Cosine for situations where the *direction* of a feature vector matters more than its magnitude (notably text and embeddings) — recognizing that the choice of distance metric is itself a meaningful modeling decision, not an arbitrary technical default.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.how_it_works: **Euclidean (L2)**: d(x,y) = √(Σ(xᵢ−yᵢ)²) — straight-line distance, the most intuitive and common default, sensitive to large individual feature differences (squaring amplifies them). **Manhattan (L1)**: d(x,y) = Σ|xᵢ−yᵢ| — sum of absolute coordinate differences, like navigating a city grid; less sensitive to large individual outlying differences (no squaring), often more robust in high-dimensional or sparse settings. **Minkowski**: d(x,y) = (Σ|xᵢ−yᵢ|^p)^(1/p) — a generalization where p=1 recovers Manhattan and p=2 recovers Euclidean, letting p be tuned as a hyperparameter to interpolate between (or extend beyond) the two. **Cosine**: similarity = (x·y)/(||x||·||y||) — measures the *angle* between vectors while ignoring their magnitudes, making it ideal when 'direction' (e.g., the relative proportions of word frequencies in a document, or the semantic orientation of an embedding) matters more than overall scale (e.g., document length); converted to a distance via 1 − cosine_similarity. The choice materially changes which points count as 'near' — two points can be Euclidean-close but Cosine-far (similar magnitude, different direction) or vice versa (very different magnitude, same direction), and this difference can flip a model's predictions entirely.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.use_when: Use Euclidean as the sensible general-purpose default for continuous, similarly-scaled numerical features; use Manhattan when robustness to large individual feature differences or high-dimensional sparsity matters; use Cosine for text, embeddings, or any setting where the *relative pattern* of feature values matters more than their absolute scale (e.g., comparing documents of very different lengths).
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.avoid_when: Avoid defaulting to Euclidean distance unreflectively on data where it doesn't naturally fit the problem's notion of similarity — e.g., applying it directly to raw word-count vectors (where document length dominates the distance) when Cosine similarity would correctly normalize away that length effect and isolate genuine topical similarity.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.what_goes_wrong: Using Euclidean distance on text represented as raw term-frequency vectors causes document *length* to dominate the distance computation — two long documents on completely different topics can appear 'closer' (in Euclidean terms) than a long and a short document on the *same* topic, simply because the long documents' vectors have larger magnitudes; Cosine similarity sidesteps this entirely by normalizing away magnitude. Applying any of these metrics to unscaled mixed-magnitude features reproduces the same scale-domination problem seen throughout distance-based methods — the metric choice doesn't fix a scaling problem, it operates *on top of* whatever scale the features are already in. Treating the metric choice as a fixed technical default rather than a tunable hyperparameter (worth comparing via cross-validation, especially for Minkowski's p) leaves performance on the table — for many problems, the 'right' notion of distance is itself something to be discovered empirically, not assumed.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.real_example: A team building a document-similarity search initially used Euclidean distance on TF-IDF vectors and found that very short documents (abstracts) were rarely matched to relevant long documents (full papers) even when topically identical — the magnitude difference between short and long documents' vectors dominated the Euclidean distance, swamping the topical-overlap signal. Switching to Cosine similarity (which normalizes by vector magnitude, focusing purely on the *direction* — i.e., the relative topical composition) immediately surfaced the correct matches regardless of document length — a textbook case where the 'natural-seeming' default distance metric was actively working against the problem's actual notion of similarity, and where understanding *why* different metrics behave differently directly translated into a one-line fix with outsized impact.

2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.what_it_is: A variant of K-Nearest Neighbours in which each neighbor's 'vote' (for classification) or contribution to the average (for regression) is weighted by its distance to the query point — typically by inverse distance (`weights='distance'` in scikit-learn) — so that closer neighbors influence the prediction more than farther ones, rather than every one of the K neighbors counting equally.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.why_it_exists: Standard (uniform-weight) KNN treats the 1st-nearest and Kth-nearest neighbor as equally informative, which is often a poor approximation — intuitively, a neighbor that's almost on top of the query point should matter more than one that's barely within the K-nearest cutoff. Weighted KNN exists to encode that intuition directly: by letting closer neighbors carry proportionally more influence, it produces smoother, often more accurate predictions, particularly in regions where neighbor distances vary substantially (dense vs. sparse regions of feature space) — all without changing K itself, effectively getting some of the benefit of a smaller K (sensitivity to close points) and a larger K (stability from considering more neighbors) simultaneously.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.how_it_works: For each of the K nearest neighbors at distance dᵢ from the query point, assign a weight wᵢ = 1/dᵢ (inverse-distance weighting — closer neighbors get exponentially larger weights as dᵢ → 0; scikit-learn handles the dᵢ = 0 edge case by giving exact matches infinite/dominant weight); the prediction becomes a weighted vote (classification: the class with the highest summed weight) or weighted average (regression: Σwᵢyᵢ / Σwᵢ) rather than a simple unweighted tally/mean. This makes the model more locally adaptive — in dense regions (where the K nearest neighbors are all very close), the weights are similar and the behavior approaches uniform KNN; in sparse regions (where neighbor distances vary widely), the few genuinely-close neighbors dominate the prediction, effectively shrinking the *functional* neighborhood size adaptively based on local data density — a useful property uniform KNN cannot replicate without manually varying K by region.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.use_when: Use when neighbor distances vary meaningfully across the dataset (data with non-uniform density, or noisy regions where you want very-close neighbors to dominate over more-distant ones included only to fill out the K count) — distance weighting is a low-cost, often-beneficial refinement over uniform voting that's simple to enable and worth comparing via cross-validation.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.avoid_when: Avoid assuming distance weighting is a strict universal improvement — on data with fairly uniform density and well-separated classes, uniform and distance weighting often perform nearly identically, and the added (mild) interpretive complexity ('why did this prediction lean so heavily on one neighbor?') isn't always worth it without measured benefit.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.what_goes_wrong: Assuming `weights='distance'` is always strictly better than `weights='uniform'` and skipping the comparison wastes a nearly-free opportunity — cross-validating both is cheap, and the better choice is genuinely data-dependent (sometimes uniform wins, especially on data with roughly-uniform density and clean class separation). Forgetting that distance weighting amplifies the importance of feature *scaling* even further than uniform KNN does — since weights are now a direct function of distance magnitude, any scale-domination issue (large-scale features dominating distance computation) doesn't just affect *which* neighbors are selected, but how strongly each one's vote counts, compounding the error. In regions with very few nearby neighbors (sparse data), distance weighting can cause a single very-close (possibly noisy/mislabeled) neighbor to dominate the prediction almost entirely — a sensitivity to individual-point noise that uniform voting (which always averages over the full K) naturally dampens.
2|🔴 T1 Classification Algorithms|Instanc.real_example: A team's uniform-weight KNN model for predicting local air-quality index showed visible 'blocky' artifacts at sensor-density boundaries — predictions changed abruptly when crossing from a sensor-dense urban area into a sensor-sparse rural one, because the K-nearest neighbors in sparse areas were much farther away on average but counted equally with close neighbors in dense areas.
