2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Statistical Methods|W.what_goes_wrong: **Leaking feature engineering into training**: applying normalization (Z-score), PCA, or lag feature extraction using statistics computed on the full series (including test data) before performing walk-forward validation is a subtle but severe data leakage form — each fold's feature engineering must be fit only on the training portion of that fold and applied to the test portion; sktime's Pipeline and TransformedTargetForecaster handle this correctly when constructed properly. **Overfitting on the validation metric**: selecting hyperparameters (ARIMA orders, regularization strength) using the walk-forward validation metric on the same series where walk-forward is also used for performance reporting creates overfitting to the validation metric; a nested cross-validation structure (outer loop: performance estimation; inner loop: hyperparameter selection) or a separate held-out test period is needed for unbiased hyperparameter tuning.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Statistical Methods|W.real_example: A forecasting team compared AutoARIMA and LightGBM on 6 months of daily store sales (182 observations). Single-split evaluation (train: days 1-150, test: 151-182): AutoARIMA MAPE=7.2%, LightGBM=6.1%. Walk-forward validation (initial window=120, step=7, h=14, 6 folds): AutoARIMA average MAPE=8.1%, LightGBM average MAPE=9.3% — LightGBM flipped to *worse* in walk-forward because its lag features required extensive history to train the ensemble effectively, and in folds with only 120-134 days of training data, LightGBM's 28-day lag features had very few valid training examples. The single-split evaluation (which happened to use 150 training days) favored LightGBM by luck; the walk-forward evaluation revealed its training-data sensitivity. AutoARIMA was deployed, and LightGBM was reconsidered when more data was available 6 months later — the walk-forward evaluation had correctly identified the data-requirement limitation that the single-split evaluation missed.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_it_is: The most fundamental time series features for ML models — past values of the target variable at specified offsets (y(t-1) = target one period ago, y(t-7) = one week ago for daily data, y(t-30) = one month ago) — which allow a standard regression model (Random Forest, XGBoost, linear regression) to use autocorrelation information by converting the temporal dependency into explicit predictor columns, enabling the model to learn 'today's value is usually near yesterday's value' or 'this week's value typically resembles last week's value at the same weekday.'
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.why_it_exists: ARIMA and ETS models encode temporal autocorrelation through the model structure (AR coefficients). ML models (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest) are pure function approximators with no built-in notion of time — they treat each row as independent. Lag features exist to bridge this gap: by creating explicit columns for y(t-k) at each relevant lag k, the time series autocorrelation information is made available to the ML model as ordinary input features, enabling it to learn the same dependencies that ARIMA captures structurally — often more flexibly (non-linear relationships, interactions between lag and other features) at the cost of requiring more data.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.how_it_works: For a pandas DataFrame `df` with datetime index and column `y`: `df['lag_1'] = df['y'].shift(1); df['lag_7'] = df['y'].shift(7); df['lag_30'] = df['y'].shift(30)`. The `.shift(k)` operation creates a new column where each row t contains y at time t-k. Rows with insufficient history (the first k observations) produce NaN — these rows must be dropped or imputed before training. Lag selection is guided by ACF plot (significant ACF at lag k → lag k is informative), domain knowledge (weekly business: lag 7 is important), and feature importance from an initial model. For panel data (multiple series), `df.groupby('series_id')['y'].shift(k)` computes lags within each series without leaking across series boundaries.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.use_when: Use lag features as the core feature set for any ML-based time series forecasting approach — they're the primary vehicle for autocorrelation information in regression-based TS models. Include lags that correspond to: (1) the dominant autocorrelation structure (ACF-guided), (2) the natural temporal rhythms in the domain (lag_7 for weekly data, lag_365 for daily data with annual seasonality), and (3) the target forecast horizon and beyond (at least lag_h where h is the forecast horizon, to ensure the lag feature is genuinely available at prediction time).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.avoid_when: Avoid including too many lag features with limited data — with 100 observations and 50 lag features, the model is severely overparameterized and will overfit; use regularization (LASSO, L2 regularization in LightGBM) or restrict to a theoretically-motivated subset of lags. Avoid lags shorter than the forecast horizon h for direct multi-step forecasting — if forecasting h=7 steps ahead, using lag_1 (the value 1 day ago) is available for 1-step forecasts but not directly available for 7-step forecasts without recursive computation; either use direct multi-step forecasting (separate model per horizon using only lags ≥ h) or recursive forecasting (accept error propagation).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_goes_wrong: **Data leakage via insufficient lag depth**: the most common error — using lag_1 (yesterday's value) to predict today's value is valid for 1-step forecasting but constitutes data leakage for 7-step forecasting (lag_1 at the 7-step forecast origin would require knowing day t-1 which is in the future relative to the forecast origin t-7). Lag depth must be at least equal to the forecast horizon for the features to be genuinely available. Not computing lags *within* each series for panel data — calling `df['lag_1'] = df['y'].shift(1)` on a panel DataFrame without grouping by series creates a lag that crosses series boundaries (the last value of series A appears as lag_1 of the first value of series B), producing training noise and test-time errors for the first observation of each series.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.real_example: An e-commerce platform modeled daily sales for 500 products using LightGBM with lag features. Initial lag set: [1, 2, 3, 7, 14, 28]. Feature importance from LightGBM: lag_7 was the highest-importance feature (82% of split gain), followed by lag_1 (9%), lag_14 (5%), with lag_2, lag_3, lag_28 together contributing only 4%. The team pruned to [1, 7, 14] and added lag_28 back later for products with monthly billing cycles. Reducing from 6 to 3 lags: model training time halved, MAPE improved from 10.2% to 9.8% (fewer features reduced overfitting on the 200 products with fewer than 100 observations). The feature importance audit — standard practice when first applying lag features — was the key diagnostic that revealed lag_7's dominance and the minimal value of the other lags for this domain.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_it_is: Time series features computed as **aggregate statistics over a trailing window** of the most recent w observations — rolling mean (moving average of the last w values), rolling standard deviation (volatility/variability of the last w periods), rolling min/max (recent range) — capturing the local level, trend, variability, and range of the series over the window, providing richer context to an ML model than point lags alone (the rolling mean captures the 'local baseline', while rolling std captures whether the series is currently in a volatile or calm period).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.why_it_exists: Single lag values are noisy — lag_7 captures one specific past value that may be an outlier, a holiday, or an anomalous week. Rolling statistics exist to provide **smoothed, aggregate summaries** of recent history that are more representative of the underlying process state: rolling_mean_7 captures the average demand over the past week (a much more stable estimate of current demand level than the single lag_7 value), and rolling_std_7 captures whether demand has been unusually variable recently (relevant for safety stock and confidence interval decisions). These features enable the ML model to condition its forecast on the current 'regime' of the series (stable high-demand period, volatile transition, declining trend).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.how_it_works: In pandas: `df['rolling_mean_7'] = df['y'].shift(1).rolling(window=7).mean()` — the `.shift(1)` is critical to prevent data leakage: it ensures the rolling window is computed on the 7 values *before* the current time step (not including the current value), so the feature is genuinely available at prediction time. Similarly: `df['rolling_std_7'] = df['y'].shift(1).rolling(7).std()`. Window sizes are typically chosen at multiples of the seasonal period (7, 14, 28 for daily data; 12, 24 for monthly data) plus domain-motivated windows. Multiple window sizes capture short-term vs. long-term local behavior: rolling_mean_7 captures current week's level, rolling_mean_90 captures the quarterly trend, rolling_std_7 captures recent volatility.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.use_when: Use rolling statistics as standard complementary features to lag features for all ML-based time series forecasting — they add information about local level and variability that isolated lag values don't capture cleanly. Include at least rolling_mean and rolling_std at one or two window sizes relevant to the data's natural temporal scale. Also useful in anomaly detection (current value vs. rolling mean in units of rolling std → z-score for anomaly scoring).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.avoid_when: Avoid very long rolling windows relative to the series length — rolling_mean_365 on a 400-observation series has only 35 valid values, and the feature is NaN for the first 365 rows, dramatically reducing the usable training set. Avoid overlapping windows that are very similar in length (rolling_mean_13, rolling_mean_14) — nearly identical features add no information while increasing feature dimensionality unnecessarily.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_goes_wrong: The most common bug: computing rolling statistics on the *current* value without shifting first — `df['rolling_mean_7'] = df['y'].rolling(7).mean()` includes y_t in the rolling window for the feature at time t, leaking the target into the feature. Always `.shift(1)` before `.rolling()` for features that should not include the current observation. Not handling the NaN values at the beginning of the rolling window — the first w observations have rolling_mean=NaN and rolling_std=NaN (insufficient history), and ML models fail with NaN features; forward-filling with the earliest available value or dropping initial rows (if data is sufficiently long) are standard approaches.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.real_example: A retail forecasting team added rolling features to a lag-only LightGBM model. Added: rolling_mean_7, rolling_mean_28, rolling_std_7, rolling_min_7, rolling_max_7 (all with .shift(1) to avoid leakage). MAPE improvement: 8.9% → 7.8% (12% relative improvement). Feature importance: rolling_mean_7 ranked 2nd after lag_7 — it provided a smoothed version of recent demand level that was more robust to single-day spikes than lag_7 alone. Rolling_std_7 ranked 5th — the model used it to predict higher demand during periods of high volatility (promotional periods with variable uplift), effectively learning that high recent variance predicts higher-than-average upcoming demand. The rolling min/max features had low importance and were removed after the importance audit, reducing model complexity without accuracy loss.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_it_is: Time series features computed as **cumulative aggregate statistics over all historical observations up to the current time** — expanding mean (average of all past values up to t), expanding standard deviation, expanding min/max — in contrast to rolling statistics (fixed window of the last w observations), expanding statistics capture the **long-run historical baseline** and evolve as more data accumulates, starting from sparse estimates early in the series and stabilizing toward the true population statistics as T grows.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.why_it_exists: Rolling statistics with a fixed window capture recent behavior but ignore the long-run history — a rolling_mean_7 for a series that has been growing for 3 years only reflects the last week's level, not the long-run trend context. Expanding statistics exist to provide the **cumulative historical context** that fixed-window rolling statistics miss: the expanding mean represents 'the average value this series has ever taken, up to this point,' which provides a useful baseline for the current forecast, and the expanding standard deviation represents 'the typical variation in this series over its entire history,' useful for anomaly detection and normalization.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.how_it_works: In pandas: `df['expanding_mean'] = df['y'].shift(1).expanding().mean()` — `.shift(1)` prevents leakage (the expanding mean up to t-1 is the feature for predicting t), `.expanding()` computes the cumulative mean from the start of the series to each time point. Similarly for `.std()`, `.min()`, `.max()`. Expanding statistics are computationally simple (O(n) operations, no window size parameter) and never produce NaN except at the very first row (where no history exists). In many applications, the expanding mean is equivalent to the 'historical mean' naive forecast and serves as a reference point for how much the current level deviates from the historical baseline.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.use_when: Use expanding statistics as long-run baseline features complementing shorter rolling windows — the combination of expanding_mean (long-run level), rolling_mean_7 (recent level), and lag_1 (yesterday's value) provides multi-scale temporal context. Particularly useful for detecting **seasonal deviation from long-run mean** (feature: current value − expanding_mean captures how much this period deviates from the historical average) and for normalization (dividing lag features by expanding_mean normalizes scale across series of different magnitudes in panel data modeling).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.avoid_when: Avoid expanding statistics when the series has strong non-stationarity (structural breaks, trending mean) — the expanding mean will be heavily influenced by the initial portion of the series and will lag the true current mean significantly; a trailing rolling window better represents the current regime for non-stationary series. Avoid using expanding statistics as the primary time series feature when the series is short (< 50 observations) — the early expanding estimates are unreliable (the expanding_std from 3 observations is a very noisy estimate of the true series volatility), and the feature stabilizes only as T grows.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_goes_wrong: Not shifting before expanding: `df['y'].expanding().mean()` includes the current observation y_t in the mean for the feature at time t — this is the same data leakage bug as rolling statistics without shifting. The fix is identical: `df['y'].shift(1).expanding().mean()`. Using expanding statistics in panel data without groupby: the expanding statistic should be computed within each series, not across all rows in the panel DataFrame; `df.groupby('series_id')['y'].shift(1).expanding().mean()` computes within-series expanding statistics correctly.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.real_example: A SaaS company modeled daily sign-ups for 200 product variants using LightGBM. For panel normalization, they divided all lag and rolling features by the expanding_mean to express them as ratios: ratio_lag_1 = lag_1 / expanding_mean (is yesterday's sign-up count above or below the historical average?). This normalization enabled a single global LightGBM model across all 200 product variants simultaneously — without normalization, products with 10,000 daily sign-ups dominated the model training and products with 50 daily sign-ups had negligible gradient contribution. With expanding_mean normalization: single model MAPE across all products = 8.1%, compared to 200 separate models' average MAPE = 7.6% (individual models slightly better) but with 1/200 the memory footprint and 1/200 the maintenance overhead — a practical tradeoff that expanding mean normalization made feasible.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_it_is: Trigonometric features — pairs of sine and cosine terms at harmonics of the seasonal frequency — that encode cyclic seasonal patterns as continuous numerical features usable by any ML model: `sin(2πkt/s)` and `cos(2πkt/s)` for k=1,2,…,K harmonics where s is the seasonal period and t is the time index, enabling smooth, continuous representation of seasonal variation that is superior to one-hot encoding of season dummies for long seasonal periods (s=365 for daily annual seasonality).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.why_it_exists: Encoding seasonality for ML models presents two choices: one-hot dummies (one feature per season position — 52 binary features for weekly annual seasonality, 365 for daily) or smooth functional forms. One-hot encoding requires 365 parameters for annual daily seasonality, is sparse, and cannot interpolate between similar season positions. Fourier features exist to provide a **compact, smooth, continuous** representation of seasonal patterns using only 2K features (K sine-cosine pairs), where K controls the flexibility of the seasonal curve — K=1 captures a simple unimodal annual pattern, K=3 captures more complex shapes with secondary peaks, K=10 approaches the flexibility of one-hot encoding but with far fewer parameters. Fourier features also handle non-integer and mixed seasonal periods (s=365.25 for leap-year-aware annual seasonality, s=7.001 for daily data with weekly non-integer period) that one-hot encoding cannot represent.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.how_it_works: For seasonal period s and K harmonics: `import numpy as np; for k in range(1, K+1): df[f'sin_{k}'] = np.sin(2*np.pi*k*t/s); df[f'cos_{k}'] = np.cos(2*np.pi*k*t/s)`. For an ML model, these 2K features encode the seasonal position smoothly. **Choosing K**: cross-validation or information criteria — K=3-5 is sufficient for most business seasonal patterns; Prophet's Fourier seasonality uses K=10 for annual and K=3 for weekly as defaults. **Multiple seasonalities**: include separate Fourier feature sets for each seasonal period — weekly and annual simultaneously: 2K₁ features for s₁=7 and 2K₂ features for s₂=365.25. The sum of all Fourier terms approximates any seasonal pattern to arbitrary accuracy as K→∞ (Fourier series convergence theorem).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.use_when: Use Fourier features as the preferred seasonality encoding for ML models when: (1) the seasonal period s is large (> 24) making one-hot encoding impractical; (2) the seasonal pattern is smooth and approximately sinusoidal (business cycles, temperature patterns, organic web traffic); (3) the data includes non-integer seasonal periods or multiple seasonalities. Fourier features are also the seasonality representation used in Prophet, TBATS, and BATS, making them the standard choice in modern forecasting.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.avoid_when: Avoid Fourier features when the seasonal pattern has sharp discontinuities — a retail series with step-changes at specific days (Black Friday spike, New Year drop) cannot be well approximated by smooth sinusoids; explicit holiday indicators should supplement or replace Fourier features for sharp calendar events. Avoid very high K for short series — with K=10 and series length T=60, the 20 Fourier features can overfit; regularization or lower K is needed.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_goes_wrong: Not normalizing the time index t before computing Fourier features — t should represent the position within the seasonal cycle (t=0 to s−1 or t/s from 0 to 1), not the absolute time since the start of the series; using the absolute time index instead of the seasonal position produces Fourier terms that don't repeat each cycle, defeating the purpose. **K too small for complex patterns**: with K=1, only the first harmonic is captured (a single sine wave per cycle) — for a seasonal pattern with both a summer peak and a winter dip (bimodal), K=2 is needed (second harmonic captures the secondary peak); K=1 would underfit and produce poor seasonal fit. Checking the seasonal pattern's frequency spectrum (Fourier transform of the seasonally-stratified series) reveals the dominant harmonics and guides K selection.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.real_example: A utility company encoded hourly electricity demand's daily seasonality (s=24) using Fourier features with K=5 (10 features: sin1...sin5, cos1...cos5). The 5 harmonics captured: fundamental (K=1: primary morning/evening peak pattern), second harmonic (K=2: asymmetry between morning and evening peak heights), and higher harmonics (K=3-5: fine details of the within-day shape). Adding Fourier features to a LightGBM model vs. 24 hour-of-day one-hot dummies: Fourier MAPE=3.1%, one-hot MAPE=3.4% — despite having only 10 features vs. 24, Fourier features produced better accuracy through regularization (fewer features, same expressive power for smooth patterns) and better generalization (smooth interpolation handles near-holiday hours that appear rarely in one-hot encoding training data).

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_it_is: Calendar-derived features extracted from the timestamp of each observation — **day of week** (DOW: 0=Monday, 6=Sunday — captures weekly seasonality and business day vs. weekend effects), **month** (1-12 — captures annual seasonality), **quarter** (1-4 — captures quarterly business patterns), and **is_holiday** (binary flag from a calendar of public holidays — captures demand anomalies on specific calendar days that regular seasonal patterns don't represent) — encoded as numerical or one-hot features that give ML models direct access to the calendar context driving the series.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.why_it_exists: Demand, traffic, and usage patterns are partly determined by the calendar — a retail store sells differently on Sundays than Mondays, differently in December than February, differently on Thanksgiving than a random Thursday. While lag features capture temporal autocorrelation and Fourier features capture smooth seasonality, datetime features provide the ML model with explicit calendar context to condition its forecast on — enabling the model to directly learn 'Sunday retail demand is 30% lower than the weekly average' or 'December 24th demand spikes 4× the baseline' rather than having to infer these patterns indirectly from lag features.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.how_it_works: From a pandas DatetimeIndex: `df['dow'] = df.index.dayofweek; df['month'] = df.index.month; df['quarter'] = df.index.quarter; df['is_weekend'] = (df.index.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int)`. For holidays: `pip install holidays; import holidays; us_holidays = holidays.US(years=range(2019, 2024)); df['is_holiday'] = df.index.normalize().isin(us_holidays).astype(int)`. Holiday libraries include national holidays; business-specific events (promotions, marketing campaigns, store openings) are typically added manually. **Encoding**: DOW and month as ordinal integers (0-6, 1-12) work with tree-based models that handle ordinal encoding natively; for linear models, one-hot encoding is needed. Alternatively, replace DOW and month with Fourier features for smooth cyclic encoding.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.use_when: Include DOW and is_holiday as standard features for daily (or sub-daily) time series where business day/weekend differences and holiday effects are present. Include month and quarter for monthly or weekly series with annual patterns when Fourier features are not used. Holiday features are particularly important for demand forecasting: holidays are known future events with large, predictable demand effects — including them as features at forecast time (using the future holiday calendar) provides information unavailable from historical patterns alone.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.avoid_when: Avoid using ordinal day-of-week (0-6) directly with linear models or distance-based models — these treat 'Monday (0)' as numerically close to 'Tuesday (1)' and 'Sunday (6)' as far from 'Saturday (5)', but Sunday and Saturday are both weekends and should be treated similarly; one-hot encoding or Fourier features avoid this spurious ordinal relationship. Avoid including all datetime features indiscriminately — quarter and month together are highly collinear (month fully determines quarter); include one or the other, not both.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_goes_wrong: Using test-time holiday indicators based on observed data rather than the holiday calendar — the holiday indicator at prediction time must come from the *future* calendar (holidays are known in advance), not from observed demand spikes; confusing these sources can cause is_holiday to be 0 in the test set for known holidays if the calendar isn't correctly applied to the future. **Encoding local vs. national holidays incorrectly**: national holiday calendars miss important local effects (Canadian Thanksgiving in October vs. US Thanksgiving in November; local school breaks); using the wrong holiday calendar can produce negative feature values (days treated as holidays when they aren't locally) that harm model accuracy.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.real_example: A food delivery platform modeled hourly orders with features: hour_of_day (as sin/cos Fourier pairs), day_of_week (one-hot), month (one-hot), is_holiday (national + local), and a 'near_holiday' flag (binary for the day before and after a holiday — captured the distinct demand pattern of pre-holiday preparation and post-holiday recovery). Without the holiday and near_holiday features: MAPE=8.4%. With just is_holiday: MAPE=7.1%. Adding near_holiday: MAPE=6.6%. The near_holiday feature was discovered by examining residuals from the is_holiday model — systematic large positive residuals on the day before Thanksgiving and Christmas revealed that pre-holiday demand was elevated even when the holiday itself wasn't yet active, suggesting the 'preparation' behavior. Engineering features directly from residual analysis (finding systematic error patterns and creating features to explain them) is a generalizable FE strategy applicable beyond this specific example.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_it_is: Time-varying features that encode the **temporal distance to a relevant past or future event** — e.g., 'days since last promotion', 'days until next holiday', 'days since last product launch', 'days since last stockout' — capturing the time-decay of event effects (promotions have diminishing carry-over impact over time) and the lead-up ramp to future events (demand increases in the days approaching a holiday) in a continuous feature that an ML model can use to learn the temporal shape of event effects.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.why_it_exists: Binary event indicators (is_holiday: 0 or 1) tell the model whether an event is occurring today but don't capture the temporal dynamics around the event — that demand starts rising 3 days before a holiday and the post-holiday hangover lasts 2 days, or that a promotion's effect decays roughly exponentially over 2 weeks. Days-since/days-until features exist to encode these temporal dynamics: by providing the continuous distance to events, the ML model can learn 'demand is elevated by X% when a promotion was 1 day ago, X%/2 when 2 days ago, X%/4 when 3 days ago' — capturing carry-over and lead-up effects that point-in-time binary indicators cannot represent.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.how_it_works: **Days since last event**: for each observation at time t, compute the number of days elapsed since the most recent event occurrence. If promotion dates are in a list `promo_dates`: `def days_since(t, events): prev_events = [e for e in events if e <= t]; return (t - max(prev_events)).days if prev_events else 999`. Apply to the index: `df['days_since_promo'] = df.index.map(lambda t: days_since(t, promo_dates))`. Capped at a maximum value (e.g., 30) to prevent unbounded values in sparse event calendars. **Days until next event**: `def days_until(t, events): future_events = [e for e in events if e > t]; return (min(future_events) - t).days if future_events else 999`. These features require the future event calendar to be known at forecast time (which is often the case for planned promotions and fixed holidays).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.use_when: Use days-since and days-until features for any series where known events have temporal carry-over or lead-up effects: promotional lift modeling (carry-over), pre-holiday demand ramp-up, post-event demand hangover, seasonal product launch (distance from seasonal peak), or operational events (days since last service disruption affecting demand). Essential in retail demand forecasting where promotion and holiday effects have complex temporal shapes.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.avoid_when: Avoid days-until features when future events are not reliably known at forecast time — using planned promotional dates that frequently change creates inconsistency between training (actual dates) and forecast (planned dates that may not happen), degrading model performance; in this case, a binary 'is promotion planned in next 7 days' feature (which can be updated if plans change) is more robust. Avoid when event frequency is very high relative to the series — for hourly data with multiple events per day, 'hours since last event' is nearly always 0 and provides little information; aggregating to daily events or using event counts per period is more informative.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_goes_wrong: Not capping days-since at a maximum — for events that occur infrequently or never in some periods, days_since can become arbitrarily large (days_since_last_promotion = 500 if there's been no promotion in 500 days), producing outlier feature values that destabilize tree model splits; capping at 30-60 days (the typical carry-over duration) produces a more stable feature. **Leaking future event information in training**: days_until_next_holiday computed at time t includes information about the exact timing of future holidays — this is legitimate (holidays are known in advance) but promotional days_until features must use the *planned* promotion calendar, not the *actual* calendar; using actual promotion dates creates leakage for training points where the model effectively knew which promotions 'would happen.'
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.real_example: A European grocery chain modeled weekly store sales with promotional events. Adding 'days since last flyer mention' (how many days ago the product appeared in the weekly promotional flyer): MAPE improved from 9.1% to 7.8%. Further adding 'days until next flyer mention' (pre-awareness effect — demand ramps up slightly before promotions): MAPE improved to 7.3%. Feature importance: days_since_promo ranked 3rd (after lag_7 and rolling_mean_4), days_until_promo ranked 7th. The model learned a clear exponential decay pattern: days_since_promo=0 (promo week) showed +45% lift, =1 week +18%, =2 weeks +8%, =3 weeks +2% (near baseline) — a 3-week carry-over pattern that the binary is_promo feature (only capturing the in-promo-week effect) had completely missed in the previous model version.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_it_is: A technique for encoding high-cardinality categorical variables (store ID, product ID, region, customer segment) as numerical features representing the **historical average of the target variable** for that category — replacing each categorical value with its historical mean target value — adapted for time series to prevent **data leakage**: computing the encoding using only past observations (strictly before the current time step) rather than the full dataset, so the encoding at time t reflects only history up to t-1.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.why_it_exists: ML models cannot directly use high-cardinality categoricals (1,000 store IDs as one-hot encoding creates 1,000 near-zero features). Target encoding compresses category information into a single informative numerical feature: 'stores with historically high sales have higher encoded values, suggesting they'll have higher sales tomorrow.' For non-temporal data, target encoding uses out-of-fold statistics to prevent leakage. For time series, **temporal ordering provides the natural validation split**: encoding must use only past observations to prevent leakage from future observations — computing the store's mean sales using all its historical data *up to* the current date prevents future data from informing the encoding of current predictions.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.how_it_works: **Naive (leaking) approach**: `target_enc[store_id] = df.groupby('store_id')['y'].mean()` — uses all observations including future ones. **Correct temporal approach**: for each time step t and store s, compute `enc[s, t] = mean(y[store==s, time < t])` — an expanding window mean over past observations only. Implementation: `df.sort_values('date').groupby('store_id')['y'].transform(lambda x: x.shift(1).expanding().mean())`. For panel forecasting where encoding is recomputed at each training cutoff, this can be done at training time: `target_enc = train_df.groupby('store_id')['y'].mean()` (the training set ends before the test set — no leakage since training data doesn't include test-period observations). **Smoothing**: `smoothed_enc = (count * cat_mean + m * global_mean) / (count + m)` where m is a smoothing strength hyperparameter — prevents high variance for categories with few observations (new stores with only 5 observations have their encoding pulled toward the global mean).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.use_when: Use temporal target encoding for panel time series ML models where categorical identifiers (store, product, SKU, customer segment) represent high-cardinality groups with meaningfully different average target levels — the encoded value provides a 'baseline level' for each entity that helps the model scale its predictions appropriately for different entity types.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.avoid_when: Avoid static target encoding (global category mean) when the target values for categories are non-stationary (a store's average sales in 2018 may not be representative of its sales in 2023 due to growth or decline); use a trailing rolling window encoding (e.g., last 4 weeks' mean for this store) rather than the all-time mean, which captures the current entity baseline more accurately than a potentially stale historical average.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_goes_wrong: The fundamental leakage bug: computing target encoding on the full dataset (including test period data) before the train/test split — this produces a target encoding for each category that includes future information, leading to models that appear accurate in cross-validation but fail in deployment because the deployed encoding can't include future data. The fix is always to compute the encoding exclusively from training data (observations before the forecast cutoff). **Cold start for new categories**: a store or product that didn't exist during training has no historical encoding — using the global mean or a similar-entity encoding as a fallback handles this, but models should be explicitly tested on held-out new categories to verify their cold-start performance.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.real_example: An e-commerce team built a LightGBM model forecasting daily GMV for 2,000 seller IDs. Using global target encoding (mean GMV per seller over the full dataset): cross-validation MAPE=5.3%; live test MAPE=8.7% — a large gap indicating leakage. Switching to expanding-window temporal target encoding (mean GMV for each seller using only observations before the current date): cross-validation MAPE=7.1%, live test MAPE=7.4% — the CV-test gap collapsed to near zero, confirming the leakage was eliminated. The encoding also incorporated smoothing (m=50) to stabilize encodings for sellers with fewer than 100 historical observations (pulling their mean toward the global average), which reduced the MAPE for new/small sellers from 12.1% to 9.4% by preventing encoding overfitting to a handful of observations.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_it_is: The application of forecast reconciliation techniques (see Optimal reconciliation entry) to **feature engineering** for time series ML models — specifically, using upper-level aggregate forecasts or aggregate statistics (from the hierarchy) as **features** for lower-level models, enabling lower-level models to condition their predictions on the aggregate context and produce forecasts that are more naturally consistent with the aggregate-level predictions, even before any formal post-hoc reconciliation step is applied.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.why_it_exists: In hierarchical forecasting, lower-level series (individual SKUs) are noisier and harder to forecast than their aggregates (product categories, regions). Adding upper-level information as features to lower-level models enables the lower-level model to use the 'wisdom of aggregates' — if the category-level forecast predicts strong growth next quarter, individual SKUs in that category should likely also grow, and the SKU-level model can adjust its forecast accordingly. This top-down information flow (in feature form) complements the bottom-up summation that hierarchical methods use, often improving both lower-level accuracy and aggregate coherence before explicit reconciliation.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.how_it_works: **Aggregate as feature**: for each SKU-level observation, join the corresponding category-level and national-level lag values as features: `sku_df = sku_df.merge(category_df[['date', 'category', 'cat_lag_1', 'cat_rolling_mean_7']], on=['date', 'category'])`. The SKU model now has access to 'what was the category-level demand last week?' as an explicit feature — providing context that the SKU's own noisy lag cannot reliably provide. **Share features**: `sku_df['sku_share'] = lag_1 / cat_lag_1` — the SKU's recent market share within its category — which captures the SKU's competitive position and predicts whether it'll capture more or less category demand in the future. **Reconciliation as post-processing**: after generating ML forecasts at all levels, apply optimal reconciliation (MinT, WLS) to ensure coherence — the feature engineering step provides more accurate base forecasts that produce better-reconciled results.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.use_when: Use aggregate features when forecasting hierarchical panel data where upper-level series are more reliable than lower-level series — retail demand forecasting (category-level smoother than SKU-level), energy demand (regional demand smoother than household-level), web traffic (site-level smoother than page-level). Including share features (SKU/category ratio) captures competitive dynamics that purely SKU-level lag features miss.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.avoid_when: Avoid aggregate features if they create endogeneity — if the aggregate is computed from all SKUs including the one being forecast, including the aggregate as a feature introduces the current-period target into the feature set (the SKU contributes to the category aggregate, so the category aggregate contains the SKU's own value for the current period). Either use the aggregate excluding the focal SKU, or use lagged aggregate values (category lag_1, not current category value) to avoid this circularity.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.what_goes_wrong: Not handling the temporal lag correctly in aggregate features — using the current-period aggregate (category sales today) as a feature for predicting today's SKU sales introduces data leakage if the aggregate is computed from all SKUs including the one being predicted; always use lagged aggregate values or leave-one-out aggregates at the SKU level. Joining aggregate features incorrectly on the date dimension — joining on the forecast date when the aggregate feature is the training aggregate (different temporal reference) produces misaligned features that degrade model performance in subtle ways that aren't immediately apparent from training metrics.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|Feature Engineering f.real_example: A CPG manufacturer forecast weekly sell-out for 5,000 products across 8 country markets. SKU×country models initially used only SKU-level lag features (MAPE=14.7%). Adding country-level aggregate features (country's total category revenue lag_1, lag_7, rolling_mean_4) and SKU market share within country: MAPE improved to 11.9% — a 19% reduction. Feature importance showed: SKU lag_1 (highest), country_category_lag_7 (second), sku_share (third) — the category-level feature was the second most important predictor, demonstrating that SKU demand is strongly driven by category-level trends that cross-country patterns capture more stably than noisy individual SKU history. The market share feature captured SKU-specific positioning changes: SKUs with declining share trends were forecast to grow below category rate, while SKUs with increasing share were forecast to grow above — a competitive dynamic invisible to lag-only models.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_it_is: The application of gradient boosting models (XGBoost, LightGBM) to time series forecasting by treating it as a tabular supervised regression problem — where each training example is (lag_1, lag_7, lag_14, rolling_mean_7, DOW, month, exogenous features) → target_y — converting the temporal forecasting problem into a standard ML regression problem and using gradient boosting's powerful non-linear, interaction-capturing capabilities to model the complex relationships between historical features and the forecast target.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.why_it_exists: ARIMA and ETS are linear models — they can capture linear autocorrelation but not interactions between lag values (does the effect of last week's value depend on the current season?) or non-linear patterns (does demand spike more in December when the preceding November was above average?). Gradient boosting with lag features exists to capture these non-linear and interaction effects while also leveraging the wealth of external features (promotions, calendar, weather, economic indicators) that standard time series models handle awkwardly. Empirically, gradient boosting with well-engineered lag features frequently outperforms ARIMA and ETS on medium-to-long series in M4, M5 and Kaggle forecasting competitions — particularly when external features add genuine predictive value.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.how_it_works: **Feature matrix construction**: for each time step t, create a row with lag features (y_{t-1}, y_{t-7}, …), rolling statistics (rolling_mean_7, rolling_std_14), datetime features (dow, month, is_holiday), and exogenous variables (price, promotion, temperature). **Direct multi-step forecasting**: train a separate model for each horizon h — model for h=1 is trained to predict y_t from features at t-1; model for h=7 is trained to predict y_t from features at t-7, using only lags ≥ 7 to avoid leakage. Alternatively, recursive forecasting: train a single h=1 model, apply it repeatedly (feeding predicted values as lag features for subsequent steps) — simpler but error-accumulating. **Hyperparameter guidance for TS**: `LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=6, min_child_samples=20, colsample_bytree=0.8, subsample=0.8, reg_alpha=0.1, reg_lambda=1.0)` — similar to Kaggle time series winning setups; tune via walk-forward CV.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.use_when: Use LightGBM/XGBoost with lag features as the primary ML forecasting approach for medium-to-long series (≥500 observations) with: multiple external features (promotions, weather, events), complex non-linear seasonality, or panel data where a single model across many series is desired (global models). Particularly effective in M5-style retail demand forecasting where promotions, prices, and product hierarchies interact with temporal patterns in complex ways that ARIMA cannot capture.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.avoid_when: Avoid for very short series (< 100 observations) where there isn't enough data to train a reliable gradient boosting model with multiple lag features — ARIMA and ETS are more appropriate. Avoid when interpretability is paramount (must explain individual forecasts to stakeholders) — gradient boosting with lag features produces SHAP-explainable forecasts but the explanation requires TS-aware interpretation of lag importance that non-technical audiences find difficult.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_goes_wrong: **The most common bug: temporal data leakage** — using any feature derived from the target at time ≥ t when predicting time t. This includes: using rolling statistics computed on the current period, using lag_1 for a direct h=7 forecast (lag_1 at forecast time t is y_{t-1}, which is 6 days after the forecast origin t-7 and therefore in the future), using target encoding computed on the full dataset. Walk-forward validation that shows dramatically better CV accuracy than live test accuracy is the primary symptom of leakage. **Over-tuning on CV**: tuning all LightGBM hyperparameters on the walk-forward CV metric on the same series used for performance reporting overfits to the specific validation split; use nested CV or a separate held-out test period for final evaluation.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.real_example: The M5 Walmart Sales competition (2020, 42,840 time series, daily sales over 5 years) was dominated by LightGBM with lag features: the winning solution used LightGBM with lags [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,14,21,28,56], rolling means [7,14,28,56], target encoding by item/store/category, and Fourier features for annual seasonality. No SARIMA or ETS model came close to the winning WRMSSE score — the complexity of promotions, price interactions, and non-linear seasonality patterns favored gradient boosting over statistical methods by a wide margin on this large-N panel dataset. The winning model was retrained without any advanced NN components, demonstrating that well-engineered LightGBM with lag features on large retail panels is harder to beat than most deep learning alternatives.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_it_is: An open-source forecasting library by Meta (Facebook) that models time series as a decomposition of **trend** (piecewise linear or logistic growth with automatic changepoint detection), **seasonality** (Fourier series representations for annual, weekly, and custom seasonal periods), and **holidays** (arbitrary user-specified holiday effects with optional day-before/day-after windows) — fitting the decomposition model via MAP estimation (using Stan's optimization) and providing uncertainty intervals via full Bayesian posterior sampling.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.why_it_exists: Business analysts with domain knowledge but limited time series modeling expertise need forecasting tools that work out of the box for the typical business use case: a series with trend, seasonal patterns, and predictable calendar events. Prophet exists to bridge this gap: it handles the most common business forecasting challenges automatically (trend changepoints, annual/weekly seasonality, holiday effects) with sensible defaults and intuitive, controllable parameters — providing much better out-of-box results than AutoARIMA for business series with strong calendar effects, while remaining accessible to non-statisticians through its Python/R interface.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.how_it_works: **Model**: y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + ε_t, where g(t) is trend (piecewise linear: y = k + at + δ·s(t) with δ as changepoint adjustments, or logistic: y = L/(1+exp(−k(t−m)))); s(t) is seasonality (Fourier series: Σⱼ (aⱼ sin(2πjt/P) + bⱼ cos(2πjt/P))); h(t) is holiday effects (indicator dummies for specified dates with optional spread windows). **Fitting**: MAP estimation of all parameters using L-BFGS on the full posterior (fast, deterministic); MCMC sampling for full uncertainty (slow, probabilistic). **Automatic changepoint detection**: `n_changepoints` evenly-spaced potential changepoints in the first 80% of the series; regularization penalizes large δ values (most changepoints will have δ≈0); `changepoint_prior_scale` controls sensitivity. **Python**: `from prophet import Prophet; model = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=True, holidays=holiday_df); model.fit(df); future = model.make_future_dataframe(periods=365); forecast = model.predict(future)`. The `forecast` DataFrame contains `yhat`, `yhat_lower`, `yhat_upper`, `trend`, `trend_lower`, `trend_upper`, plus component columns.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.use_when: Use Prophet for: (1) business time series with daily or sub-daily frequency where annual and weekly seasonality, holidays, and trend changepoints are the dominant drivers; (2) non-statistician audiences who need to tune forecasts through interpretable parameters (adjust seasonality strength, add custom events) rather than ARIMA p,d,q notation; (3) quick prototyping where a reasonable baseline is needed without manual feature engineering. Prophet excels for website traffic, revenue, and social media metrics — the use cases it was designed for at Meta.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.avoid_when: Avoid Prophet for sub-hourly data (it doesn't handle sub-daily seasonality natively without custom Fourier terms), for series with complex multivariate effects (no regression component beyond the limited `add_regressor` functionality), or for series where the Fourier + piecewise linear decomposition is a poor structural match (e.g., financial return series, series with heavy autocorrelation in residuals). M competition results show Prophet underperforming AutoETS and AutoARIMA on aggregate — it's not a competitive choice for pure statistical forecasting of arbitrary series.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_goes_wrong: **Over-sensitive changepoint detection**: with `changepoint_prior_scale` too high, Prophet fits every small fluctuation as a changepoint and the trend oscillates wildly — visually obvious as a trend that zigzags within the training data and extrapolates into impossible future values. The default `changepoint_prior_scale=0.05` is conservative; raise it only when trend genuinely changes frequently. **Holiday not in the forecast horizon**: if `holidays` DataFrame only covers historical dates and not the future forecast period, Prophet's holiday component is zero for all future predictions — always ensure `holidays` extends at least as far forward as the forecast horizon. Not checking that Prophet's residuals are white noise — significant ACF in residuals means Prophet hasn't fully captured the autocorrelation structure; consider adding an AR term via `add_regressor` or switching to a model that explicitly captures autocorrelation.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.real_example: Airbnb's data science team used Prophet for internal business metric forecasting — daily booking volume, revenue, and host sign-ups. Key customizations: (1) custom seasonality for the 'Airbnb year' (heavier summer and winter holiday weights than default); (2) manual changepoints for major product launches; (3) holiday effects for 60+ country holiday calendars for the international time series. Prophet allowed Airbnb's data analysts (not ML engineers) to forecast their own metrics with high accuracy — the interpretable decomposition (trend + seasonality + holidays) let analysts understand and explain forecast deviations, catching anomalies by comparing actuals to the expected decomposition component values. The key limitation encountered: for markets with >12 months seasonal patterns (annual booking cycles in academic markets tied to university terms), the default annual Fourier seasonality needed manual augmentation with K=6 harmonics to capture the bimodal booking pattern.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_it_is: An evolution of Prophet that replaces Prophet's simple additive error structure with a **neural network-based autoregressive component** — combining Prophet's interpretable trend + seasonality + holidays decomposition with an AR-Net (a simple feedforward neural network taking lag features as inputs) that captures residual autocorrelation structure the standard Prophet decomposition leaves unexplained, while maintaining Prophet's fitting framework and a similar Python API.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.why_it_exists: Prophet's residuals often exhibit significant autocorrelation — the decomposition captures trend, seasonality, and holiday effects but leaves the autocorrelation structure in the residuals unexplained. Adding an autoregressive component addresses this, but a simple AR model (linear combination of lags) may miss non-linear lag dependencies. NeuralProphet exists to add a learned non-linear AR component (the AR-Net) on top of Prophet's decomposition, improving forecast accuracy for series where the residuals after the Prophet decomposition have exploitable autocorrelation structure — particularly relevant for medium-to-high-frequency series where AR structure is strong.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.how_it_works: **Model**: y(t) = trend(t) + seasonality(t) + events(t) + f(y_{t-1}, …, y_{t-p}) + ε_t, where f(·) is a shallow feedforward neural network with p lag inputs, hidden layers (typically 1-2 layers, 64 nodes), and a scalar output capturing the autocorrelation component. **Training**: uses PyTorch and optimizes all components jointly by stochastic gradient descent (Adam optimizer) — unlike Prophet's MAP/MCMC approach, NeuralProphet is trained end-to-end with backpropagation. **Key parameters**: `n_lags` controls the AR order (how many lags to include), `n_forecasts` enables direct multi-step forecasting (training all h-step models simultaneously), `n_changepoints` and Fourier seasonality orders similar to Prophet. **Python**: `from neuralprophet import NeuralProphet; model = NeuralProphet(n_lags=7, n_forecasts=14, yearly_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=True); model.fit(df); future = model.make_future_dataframe(df, periods=14); forecast = model.predict(future)`.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.use_when: Use NeuralProphet over Prophet when: (1) Prophet's residuals show significant ACF (autocorrelation left uncaptured by the decomposition), (2) short-to-medium horizon forecasts where the AR-Net's learned autocorrelation captures patterns that improve over the Prophet baseline, and (3) when direct multi-step forecasting (`n_forecasts > 1`) is needed to avoid recursive forecast error accumulation.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.avoid_when: Avoid NeuralProphet for very short series (< 100 observations) where the neural network component (AR-Net) has insufficient data to train reliably — the Prophet decomposition without neural AR is more reliable with limited data. Avoid for series where the AR component is expected to be simple and linear — a basic SARIMA or Prophet + manual AR regressor may outperform NeuralProphet at a fraction of the computational cost and training complexity.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_goes_wrong: NeuralProphet requires careful `epochs` and `learning_rate` tuning — the default training may either under-converge (stopping too early, producing a poor fit) or over-fit if epochs are too high and the dataset is small; monitoring the training loss curve and using early stopping is recommended. Unlike Prophet which uses MAP estimation and rarely fails, NeuralProphet's gradient descent can get stuck in local optima or diverge with poor initialization — running with multiple random seeds and selecting the best result (by validation loss) is recommended for production use.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.real_example: An energy forecaster compared Prophet and NeuralProphet for hourly electricity demand forecasting (2 years of hourly data, 17,520 observations). Prophet MAPE = 4.2% on a 24-hour forecast horizon; residual ACF showed significant spikes at lags 1-3 (strong short-term autocorrelation). NeuralProphet with n_lags=24, n_forecasts=24: MAPE = 3.1% — a 26% improvement driven by the AR-Net capturing the residual hour-to-hour autocorrelation that Prophet left unexplained. NeuralProphet's direct multi-step forecasting (all 24 hours trained simultaneously) also eliminated the recursive error accumulation that would have occurred with a 1-step Prophet + manual recursion approach for 24-hour forecasting, contributing an additional ~0.3% MAPE improvement over recursive Prophet.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_it_is: **Long Short-Term Memory** networks applied to time series forecasting — a recurrent neural network architecture with gated memory cells (input gate, forget gate, output gate) that enables learning long-range temporal dependencies in sequential data, used to forecast future values of a time series by processing the history as a sequence and producing a forecast from the final hidden state — a foundational approach to neural time series forecasting that preceded the Transformer era.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.why_it_exists: Standard feedforward networks with fixed lag features can only capture fixed-length window patterns. Simple RNNs theoretically have infinite memory but suffer from vanishing gradients when trained on long sequences. LSTMs exist to solve the vanishing gradient problem for sequence modeling: the gated architecture explicitly controls what information to retain (remember gate) and what to discard (forget gate) across arbitrary sequence lengths, enabling the network to learn long-range dependencies (e.g., 'the demand pattern from the same week last year affects this week's forecast') that fixed-window feedforward approaches cannot capture.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.how_it_works: **LSTM cell**: for each time step t, four computations: forget gate f_t = σ(W_f·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f); input gate i_t = σ(W_i·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i); candidate cell C̃_t = tanh(W_C·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_C); cell state update C_t = f_t⊙C_{t-1} + i_t⊙C̃_t; output h_t = σ(W_o·[h_{t-1}, x_t])⊙tanh(C_t). **For forecasting**: encode the historical sequence (y_{t-L}, …, y_{t-1}, x_{t-L}, …, x_{t-1}) through an LSTM encoder to produce a context vector h_T; decode with an LSTM decoder or linear layer to produce forecasts ŷ_{t+1}, …, ŷ_{t+h}. **Training**: BPTT (backpropagation through time) via PyTorch or TensorFlow; `torch.nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers)`. The note references 'covered in DL phase' — Phase 3/4 will cover deep learning architectures in detail; the key TS-relevant context is that LSTM has largely been superseded by Transformer-based models (TFT, PatchTST, Mamba) for time series in recent research but remains widely used in production due to simpler training and serving.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.use_when: Use LSTM for sequence-to-sequence time series forecasting when temporal dependencies are genuinely long-range (beyond what fixed-window lag features capture) and sufficient training data is available (≥1,000 time steps per series, or a large panel of series for global LSTM training). Encoder-decoder LSTMs remain competitive for univariate and multivariate forecasting when the context length (number of historical steps) is long relative to the forecast horizon.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.avoid_when: Avoid LSTM as the first choice for time series forecasting — Temporal Fusion Transformer, N-BEATS, and Transformer variants consistently outperform LSTM on standard benchmarks (ETTh1, ETTm1, M4, M5) while being similarly or less expensive to train. For production systems already using LSTM, the migration cost to TFT may not be justified unless accuracy improvements are demonstrated on the specific use case.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_goes_wrong: **Vanishing/exploding gradients**: even with LSTM's gated architecture, very long sequences (L > 500) can cause training instability; gradient clipping (`torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)`) and normalized inputs are standard mitigations. **Teacher forcing vs. scheduled sampling**: training with 'teacher forcing' (feeding actual values as inputs during training) but forecasting with 'free running' (feeding predicted values as inputs) creates a train/test discrepancy that degrades multi-step forecast quality — scheduled sampling (gradually replacing teacher forcing with predicted values during training) mitigates this mismatch.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.real_example: An IoT company used LSTM to forecast server load 1 hour ahead from 6 months of 1-minute resolution CPU utilization data. A 2-layer LSTM with hidden_size=128, context length=60 minutes, trained with Adam optimizer (lr=0.001) achieved 3.8% MAPE — compared to AutoARIMA's 6.1% on the same data. The improvement stemmed from the LSTM capturing non-linear interaction between CPU utilization patterns (e.g., load spikes that follow specific usage patterns from 45 minutes prior — a pattern too subtle for ACF analysis to identify cleanly as a lag feature, but learnable from the gated memory of the LSTM encoder).

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_it_is: A deep learning architecture for multi-horizon time series forecasting that combines **variable selection networks** (learned importance weights for input features), **gating mechanisms** (skip connections that allow the model to ignore irrelevant components), **LSTM encoders** (for processing the known past sequence), **static covariate encoders** (for entity-level features that don't change over time), and **multi-head self-attention** (for identifying long-range temporal patterns) with interpretable attention weights that reveal which historical time steps were most influential for each forecast — producing both accurate probabilistic (quantile) forecasts and interpretable attention-based explanations.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.why_it_exists: Existing deep learning forecasters (DeepAR, LSTM) are either accurate but opaque or interpretable but less accurate. TFT (Lim et al., 2021, Google Research) exists to achieve both simultaneously by incorporating attention mechanisms that are inherently interpretable (attention weights show which time steps the model focused on) and variable selection networks that indicate which input features were most important for each series at each time step — addressing the business requirement that complex models must provide explanations alongside predictions, not just accuracy metrics.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.how_it_works: **Input types**: static covariates (entity-level unchanging attributes — product category, store region), known future inputs (features known for the full forecast horizon — day of week, holidays, planned promotions), and observed past inputs (features known only in the past — historical demand, price). **Architecture**: (1) Input preprocessing: variable selection networks learn which inputs are most relevant, suppressing irrelevant features via gating; (2) Past sequence encoding: LSTM processes the historical window with selected inputs; (3) Attention: multi-head attention over the LSTM encoder outputs identifies which historical time steps (e.g., 'same day last year' or 'last week') are most informative for the forecast; (4) Output: position-wise feedforward network produces quantile forecasts at all forecast horizons simultaneously. **Python**: `from pytorch_forecasting import TemporalFusionTransformer, TimeSeriesDataSet; dataset = TimeSeriesDataSet(df, target='y', ...); tft = TemporalFusionTransformer.from_dataset(dataset, ...); trainer = pl.Trainer(...); trainer.fit(tft, train_dataloader, val_dataloader)`.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.use_when: Use TFT when: (1) multivariate forecasting with multiple feature types (static entity attributes, known future features, historical covariates) and the interaction effects between them are expected to be important; (2) interpretability is needed alongside accuracy — the attention weights and variable importance provide business-meaningful explanations; (3) probabilistic (quantile) forecasts are needed for downstream optimization (safety stock, pricing under uncertainty); (4) sufficient data is available (TFT's architecture has many parameters; a minimum of ~10,000 training examples is recommended).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.avoid_when: Avoid TFT for simple univariate forecasting without external features — its complex architecture provides no advantage over simpler models when the additional complexity isn't warranted by the input feature richness. Avoid when training data is very limited (< 5,000 examples) — TFT has many parameters (attention layers, variable selection networks) and will overfit with insufficient data.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_goes_wrong: TFT requires careful data formatting in `pytorch-forecasting`'s `TimeSeriesDataSet`: static, known-future, and observed-past covariates must be correctly classified, and the `max_encoder_length` (context window) and `max_prediction_length` (forecast horizon) must be set appropriately — errors here produce models that appear to train but have degraded accuracy due to incorrect temporal masking or feature alignment. **Training instability**: TFT uses many gating and normalization components that can produce NaN loss values with inappropriate learning rates; always use a learning rate finder (`Trainer.tuner.lr_find(tft, train_dataloader)`) before training and clip gradients (`gradient_clip_val=0.1` in PyTorch Lightning Trainer).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.real_example: Zillow's demand forecasting team used TFT to forecast 6-month home price appreciation at the ZIP code level, with static covariates (ZIP demographics, housing stock characteristics), known future inputs (macroeconomic forecasts, planned infrastructure projects), and observed past inputs (historical price changes, inventory levels, days-on-market). TFT achieved 12% lower MAPE than their previous LSTM baseline while also providing attention-based explanations: attention patterns revealed that the model consistently focused on the same-quarter-one-year-ago time step (~52 weeks back) for seasonal markets — a finding that validated the model's learned seasonality and provided interpretable justification for the model's output that the pure LSTM couldn't supply.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_it_is: Two pure deep learning architectures for time series forecasting — **N-BEATS** (Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for Interpretable Time Series Forecasting, Oreshkin et al., 2020) uses stacks of fully-connected residual blocks with forward and backward projections ('forecast' and 'backcast') that decompose the input into trend and seasonal basis expansions; **N-HiTS** (Neural Hierarchical Interpolation for Time Series, Challu et al., 2023) extends N-BEATS with multi-rate sampling (different stacks process the input at different temporal scales) and hierarchical interpolation of outputs — both achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on standard benchmarks with simpler architectures than attention-based models.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.why_it_exists: Transformer-based forecasters (TFT, Autoformer, Informer) add architectural complexity (attention mechanisms, positional encodings, separate encoder-decoder stacks) that doesn't always translate to accuracy improvements for time series. N-BEATS and N-HiTS exist as a counterpoint: by using simpler architecture (fully-connected residual blocks with the 'doubly residual stacking' principle) that processes the raw input series directly, they demonstrate that carefully-designed simple architectures can match or outperform much more complex Transformer variants — a finding that prompted broader scrutiny of whether Transformer-based TS models are actually justified by their accuracy improvements over simpler baselines.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.how_it_works: **N-BEATS**: the core unit is a 'block' with a 4-layer fully-connected network that takes the historical window as input and outputs two vectors: backcast (reconstruction of input) and forecast (contribution to the output). Multiple blocks are stacked in 'stacks': the first stack produces a partial backcast and forecast; the residual of the input (after subtracting the backcast) is passed to the next block, which refines the forecast. The final forecast is the sum of all blocks' forecast contributions. Interpretable variant: the last projection layer uses predefined trend polynomial or Fourier seasonal basis functions (instead of learned bases) — the block's forecast contribution is interpretable as 'the trend component' or 'the seasonal component.' **N-HiTS**: adds MaxPool downsampling at different rates across stacks (short-range patterns in one stack, long-range patterns in another) and linear interpolation of outputs to the original frequency, improving long-horizon forecast accuracy by explicitly separating scale of temporal patterns. Python: `from neuralforecast.models import NBEATS, NHiTS; from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast; nf = NeuralForecast(models=[NBEATS(input_size=2*h, h=h)], freq='D'); nf.fit(df)`.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.use_when: Use N-BEATS for medium-to-long-horizon univariate forecasting where simplicity and strong baseline accuracy are valued — N-BEATS consistently achieves top-3 performance on M4, ETT, and similar benchmarks with lower training complexity than TFT. Use N-HiTS for longer forecast horizons (h ≥ 7) where multi-scale temporal pattern separation is beneficial — N-HiTS's hierarchical interpolation specifically addresses the long-horizon performance degradation that single-rate models experience.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.avoid_when: Avoid N-BEATS/N-HiTS for multivariate forecasting where covariate features (known future inputs, static entity attributes) must be incorporated — both architectures are primarily univariate (or multivariate via concatenation without TFT-style variable selection); TFT or `pytorch-forecasting`'s multivariate models better handle rich feature sets. Avoid when training data is very short — the fully-connected blocks have many parameters and overfit on short series.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_goes_wrong: **Interpretable vs. generic N-BEATS trade-off**: the interpretable (Trend+Seasonality basis) variant has lower capacity but directly interpretable block outputs; the generic variant has higher capacity (learned bases) and better raw accuracy but loses interpretability — choosing the wrong variant for the use case (interpretable when accuracy is paramount, generic when explanations are needed) is a common suboptimal decision. Not using Nixtla's `neuralforecast` library for N-BEATS/N-HiTS implementation — the original NBEATS paper's code is harder to adapt for production than `neuralforecast`'s well-maintained, optimized implementation that integrates with the Nixtla ecosystem (same `unique_id/ds/y` data format as statsforecast, enabling easy model comparison).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.real_example: In the M4 competition (100,000 time series, yearly/quarterly/monthly/weekly/daily/hourly), N-BEATS achieved an OWA (Overall Weighted Average) of 0.873 — significantly outperforming statistical ensembles (ETS+ARIMA: OWA≈0.93) and placing among the top competitive methods. Notably, N-BEATS is a 'global model' — a single model trained on *all* 100,000 series simultaneously (not series-specific models like ARIMA) — and the global training allowed it to transfer knowledge across series, learning patterns (e.g., 'upward trends typically persist') that generalize across the diverse M4 series. This global-model property is the key advantage over statistical methods in competition settings with diverse time series, and the practical implication is that N-BEATS requires a sufficiently diverse and large training corpus to realize its global-model advantage.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_it_is: A second, distinct entry for TFT that emphasizes its three defining architectural properties as a unified description: **multivariate** (handles static entity attributes, known future covariates, and observed historical covariates jointly via variable selection networks), **attention** (multi-head self-attention over encoded history produces attention weights showing *which past time steps drove each forecast*, the primary interpretability mechanism), and **interpretable** (variable importance scores from variable selection networks reveal which features matter most for each series at each forecast step) — together making TFT the go-to architecture when you need both competitive forecasting accuracy and explainable outputs for stakeholder communication.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.why_it_exists: This entry specifically highlights the three architectural pillars that differentiate TFT from simpler deep learning forecasters: the multivariate handling is more structured than concatenation-based approaches (separate processing pipelines for static/known-future/observed-past with gated residual connections); the attention mechanism produces time-step-level explanations rather than just black-box outputs; and the interpretability is architectural (built-in) rather than post-hoc (via SHAP, which requires additional computation and assumptions). These three properties address the core business tension between model complexity and explainability.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.how_it_works: **Multivariate handling**: three input categories are each processed by dedicated variable selection networks (VSNs) — VSNs apply softmax-normalized entity-conditioned attention across feature columns, learning which features to focus on for each static entity context. **Gated Residual Networks (GRN)**: core building block throughout TFT — a non-linear transformation with a gate that can 'skip' the non-linear transformation when the component isn't useful, preventing unnecessary complexity. **Self-attention**: Q/K/V multi-head attention applied over the LSTM encoder outputs interprets the temporal context; attention weights (visualized as heatmaps over time) reveal the temporal patterns the model exploited — typically showing strong attention to same-day-last-week and same-time-last-year positions, confirming that the model learned seasonality. **Quantile output**: TFT produces q0.1, q0.5, q0.9 forecasts by default, supporting probabilistic decision-making. See the earlier TFT entry for implementation details (`pytorch-forecasting`).
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.use_when: Use when the previous TFT entry's conditions apply and the team specifically needs to communicate to business stakeholders *why* the model made a specific forecast — TFT's attention weights and variable importance provide the level of interpretability needed for regulated industries (healthcare, finance) or strategic decision-making contexts where 'the model said so' is insufficient justification for a business action.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.avoid_when: The same caveats as the previous TFT entry apply — this entry provides the architectural explanation of TFT's multivariate/attention/interpretable properties as a complement to the previous entry's implementation-focused description.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_goes_wrong: A subtle interpretability trap: TFT's attention weights are not the same as causal attribution — a high attention weight on 'one year ago' means the model found that time step informative, not that it's causally important; it could be informative because of correlated seasonal patterns rather than direct causation. Presenting attention weights as causal explanations to non-technical stakeholders can be misleading; they should be described as 'which historical time steps the model found most predictive,' not 'which time steps caused today's forecast.'
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.real_example: A financial services firm used TFT for quarterly revenue forecasting across 150 business units with known future features (planned marketing spend, product roadmap milestones), static features (business unit size, industry vertical), and observed past features (quarterly revenue, customer count, churn rate). TFT's variable importance scores revealed: customer count lag was the highest-importance feature for 82% of business units (not revenue lag), and planned marketing spend was second — an insight that shifted the firm's monitoring from revenue-tracking to customer-count-tracking as the leading indicator. The attention heatmaps showed the model focused primarily on 4-8 quarters back, confirming that long-term revenue trajectories (not just recent history) drove the most informative historical signals, consistent with the firm's understanding that enterprise revenue contracts have 1-2 year cycles.

2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.what_it_is: An autoregressive probabilistic deep learning forecasting model (Amazon Research, Salinas et al., 2020) that trains a single **global LSTM** across a large collection of related time series, conditioning forecasts on the series' history and optional covariate features, and outputs parameters of a probability distribution (typically Gaussian, Student-t, negative binomial, or beta) rather than point estimates — enabling direct sampling of probabilistic forecasts and quantile estimation for the full forecast horizon.
2|🔴 T1 Time Series|ML & Deep Learning fo.why_it_exists: Point forecasting ignores uncertainty — a forecast that 'expects' 100 units with a 95% confidence interval of [20, 340] requires very different inventory decisions than one with an interval of [85, 115]. DeepAR exists to produce calibrated probabilistic forecasts from deep learning by modeling the full conditional distribution p(y_{t+1}|y_1, …, y_t, covariates) as a parameterized distribution trained by maximum likelihood — enabling principled uncertainty quantification directly from the model rather than as a post-hoc heuristic, while also benefiting from global training across many series for improved generalization to new/sparse series.
